0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Book of Leviticus
0.overview:
Leviticus is the book most Christians skip and most preachers fear. Its pages drip with blood, smoke, and the minute regulation of altars, animals, and ailments. Yet to neglect Leviticus is to neglect the very heart of the gospel, for here, more than anywhere in the Old Testament, we learn how a sinful people may dwell with a holy God. The whole book answers a single question raised at the end of Exodus: when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle so that even Moses could not enter (Exod 40:35), how shall mortal, defiled creatures come near? Leviticus is God's gracious answer — a manual of access, written in the language of sacrifice.

The dominating word is holy. It appears more often in Leviticus than in any other book of the Bible. As R.C. Sproul never tired of insisting, holiness is not merely one of God's attributes among many; it is the very burning core of his being. The seraphim do not cry "Love, love, love" or "Mercy, mercy, mercy," but "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3). Leviticus exists to brand that threefold cry upon the conscience of a redeemed people: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2).

But Leviticus is not legalism. It stands inside grace. Israel is already redeemed; the blood of the Passover lamb has already been shed; the people have already been brought out of Egypt and into covenant at Sinai. Everything in Leviticus is for a people God has already claimed as his own. The sacrifices do not purchase God's love — they are the appointed means by which an already-loved people may live in the presence of the One who loves them. Grace precedes law, as it always does.

Above all, Leviticus is about Jesus. Every offering, every priest, every drop of blood, every Day of Atonement points beyond itself to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The book of Hebrews is the inspired commentary on Leviticus, and its message is that all these shadows have found their substance in Christ. To read Leviticus rightly is to be brought, again and again, to the foot of the cross and to whisper with adoring wonder, "It is finished." Holy, holy, holy — and yet, in Christ, the holy God has made a way for us to come home.

1.title: The Burnt Offering: Wholly the Lord's
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, <sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD... <sup>4</sup>He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. <sup>9</sup>...And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD."
1.overview:
Leviticus opens not with a command but with a calling: "The LORD called Moses." The same God whose glory had just filled the tabernacle now speaks from within it, and his first word to a redeemed people is about worship — how to draw near. The very first offering described is the burnt offering, the 'olah, the offering that ascends. It is the only sacrifice in which the entire animal, apart from the skin, is consumed upon the altar. Nothing is held back; nothing is eaten by priest or worshipper. It goes up entirely to God in smoke.

Gordon Wenham observes that the burnt offering is fundamentally an offering of total self-dedication. The worshipper is saying, in the language of fire, "All that I am I give to you." The key gesture is in verse 4: the worshipper lays his hand upon the head of the animal. This is the language of identification and substitution. As the hand presses down, the worshipper's guilt is symbolically transferred; what happens to the animal happens, by representation, to the man. The innocent dies in place of the guilty.

Sinclair Ferguson reminds us that the phrase "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" is not crude anthropomorphism but covenant language: the sacrifice is acceptable, it satisfies, it brings delight to the heart of God. And here the gospel breaks through, for Paul takes this very phrase and applies it to Christ: "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2).

The burnt offering is Christ our whole burnt offering — the one who held nothing back, who gave himself entirely to the Father on our behalf, who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7). Where our consecration is always partial, hesitant, hedged with reservations, his was total. He ascended in the flame of the Father's will and rose as the fragrance that makes us, in him, acceptable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leviticus opens where Exodus closed — with the glory of God filling the tent — and now God speaks from that glory to teach his people how to come near. The first and most fundamental sacrifice is the burnt offering (Hebrew olah, "that which ascends"), the only offering entirely consumed on the altar. Nothing is kept back; the whole animal goes up in smoke as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD." It pictures total consecration and atonement together — a life wholly given to God in the worshiper's place.
verseByVerse.theology: The burnt offering teaches substitution and total devotion. The worshiper lays his hand on the animal's head (v.4), identifying with it, transferring guilt to a substitute; the animal dies in his place and is wholly burned, expressing a life completely surrendered to God. It is the clearest Levitical picture of Christ, who "gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2), and who offered himself "without blemish to God" (Heb 9:14). And graciously, God scales the offering to the giver's means — bull, sheep, or two birds — so the poorest may still draw near.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the worshiper pressed his hand on the animal's head, felt its life given in his place, and watched it ascend wholly to God — atonement and consecration in one act of smoke.

Now: Christ is our whole burnt offering, given entirely to God for us. And in him our response is total: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God" (Rom 12:1) — not part of us, but all.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, 'Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice how the book begins: "The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting." Exodus ended with the glory of God filling the tent, so full that Moses could not enter (Ex 40:35). Now, from within that glory, God speaks — and his first concern is to teach sinners how they may come near without being consumed. That is the whole subject of Leviticus: how a holy God can be approached by an unholy people, and how they can live in his presence. And the very first word is an invitation: "when any one of you brings an offering." The Hebrew word for offering is qorban, from a root meaning "to draw near." To bring a sacrifice is to draw near to God. The book that many find forbidding actually opens with a gracious welcome — God making a way for people to come close. Every law that follows is, at heart, an answer to the deepest longing of the human soul: how can I come to God?

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish... He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him... And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The burnt offering must be "a male without blemish" — the best of the flock, unmarred, for God is worthy of the finest and because this offering points to a spotless Substitute. Then comes the decisive act: the worshiper "shall lay his hand on the head" of the animal. This is no casual gesture. It is identification and transfer — the man leaning his weight on the creature, confessing "this death is mine, this life stands in my place." And the result: "it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him." The animal dies so the sinner lives. Then the whole animal is burned, entirely consumed, rising as "a pleasing aroma to the LORD." Nothing is held back. Here, in the first chapter of Leviticus, is the gospel in miniature: a spotless substitute, a hand laid in faith, guilt transferred, life given wholly to God, atonement secured. It is the very shape of the cross, where Christ, "a lamb without blemish" (1 Pet 1:19), gave himself entirely for us (Eph 5:2).

verseByVerse.quote: If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish... and the priest shall burn it all on the altar. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same offering may be brought from the flock — a sheep or a goat — for not every Israelite owned cattle. The ritual is the same: a male without blemish, the life given, the whole burned as a pleasing aroma. What matters is not the size of the animal but the reality of the substitution and the wholeness of the devotion. God does not measure his people by their wealth. The truth is identical whether the offering is a bull or a lamb: a spotless life given in the sinner's place, ascending wholly to God. This gracious flexibility guards against a religion of the rich — the herdsman and the shepherd stand on the same ground before God, both accepted through the same atoning death.

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons... It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: And then, tenderly, God stoops lower still. If a person cannot afford even a sheep, he may bring two turtledoves or pigeons — birds that cost almost nothing, that even the poorest could catch or buy. And the astonishing thing is that the bird offering is called by the very same words as the bull: "a burnt offering... a pleasing aroma to the LORD." The poor man's two birds smell as sweet to God as the rich man's bull. No one is too poor to draw near; no one is shut out of atonement for lack of means. This is the God who would one day be presented in the temple by parents too poor to bring a lamb, who offered instead "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" (Luke 2:24) — the offering of the poor, made for the King of kings. The door to God stands open to the humblest hand.

1.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The laid-on hand and the slain victim teach that sin is dealt with not by human effort but by a divinely provided substitute. This is the spine of biblical religion and the heart of the cross.

Total consecration. The wholly consumed offering models the surrender Christ rendered to the Father and which the Spirit now works in us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).

The pleasing aroma. What the burnt offering symbolized, Christ accomplished — he is "a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2), and in him our worship rises acceptably.
1.examples:
Then: An Israelite, conscious of sin, brought a bull from his own herd, pressed his hand upon its head, and watched it die and ascend in flame — a vivid, costly, bloody lesson that approaching God requires a substitute.

Now: We come to God through the once-for-all offering of Christ. The burnt offering calls us to a worship that holds nothing back — to lay our whole selves on the altar, knowing we are already accepted in the Beloved.

2.title: The Grain Offering: The Labor of Our Hands
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it... <sup>11</sup>No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD. <sup>13</sup>You shall season all your grain offerings with salt... the salt of the covenant with your God.
2.overview:
After the bloody burnt offering comes the bloodless grain offering, the minchah — a gift, a tribute. Where the burnt offering speaks of atonement, the grain offering speaks of consecrated labor. Grain does not grow wild and ready; it is the product of plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding. To bring fine flour is to bring the fruit of one's toil, the offering of one's working life laid upon the altar of God.

Wenham notes that the grain offering often accompanied the burnt offering, so that the dedication of the self (the burnt offering) was joined to the dedication of the self's labor (the grain offering). The God who redeems us claims not only our souls but our Mondays — our work, our wages, our ordinary industry.

Three details preach. No leaven, for leaven, the fermenting agent of corruption, is throughout Scripture a symbol of sin (1 Cor 5:8). No honey, for the sweetness of the world's natural fermentation has no place on God's altar. But salt — "the salt of the covenant" — must season every offering, for salt preserves, salt does not corrupt, salt seals a covenant as an enduring bond.

And here is Christ, the true bread offered to the Father. He is the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died (John 12:24); he is the bread of life (John 6:35); his was the only human life ever lived wholly without the leaven of sin, seasoned through and through with the salt of unbreakable covenant faithfulness. The grain offering, ground fine and passed through fire, whispers of the One whose perfect life of labor and obedience was offered up, a pleasing aroma, for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the burnt offering comes the grain offering (Hebrew minchah, "gift" or "tribute") — the one offering with no blood and no death. It is fine flour with oil and frankincense, or baked cakes, a portion burned on the altar and the rest given to the priests. It expresses thanksgiving and the dedication of one's daily work and bread to God. No leaven, no honey — nothing that corrupts — but always salt, the sign of the covenant that does not spoil.
verseByVerse.theology: The grain offering consecrates the fruit of human labor — the bread we earn by the sweat of our brow given back to God in thanks (cf. Deut 26). Its ingredients preach: fine flour (nothing coarse), no leaven or honey (no corruption or mere sweetness that ferments), and always "the salt of the covenant" (v.13), a sign of permanence and fidelity (cf. Num 18:19; Mark 9:49-50). Sinless and whole, it points to Christ, the true "bread of life" (John 6:35), the grain of wheat that fell to the ground (John 12:24), whose perfect life was wholly acceptable to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the farmer brought the fruit of his fields — flour, oil, and incense — and gave it back to God, consecrating his labor and his daily bread with thanks.

Now: we offer God our ordinary work and provision as worship: "whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Cor 10:31). And we feast on the true bread, Christ, whose life was the one wholly pleasing gift to the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it... and the priest shall burn... a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons.
verseByVerse.commentary: The grain offering is unique among the sacrifices: no animal dies, no blood is shed. It is a gift of "fine flour" — the best of the harvest, finely milled — with oil poured on it and frankincense laid over it. A handful is burned as "a pleasing aroma," and the rest becomes food for the priests. What does it mean? It is the offering of the fruit of one's labor. A person could not bring a bull if he was a farmer of grain, but he could bring the work of his own hands, his daily bread, and give it back to God in thanksgiving. Here is a beautiful truth: God receives not only atonement but gratitude, not only the shedding of blood but the dedication of ordinary work. Your labor, your bread, the fruit of your week, can be laid on the altar as worship. And because it is made of fine flour, unblemished and whole, it whispers of the one perfect Life that would be wholly pleasing to God — Christ, "the bread of life" (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD... You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing.
verseByVerse.commentary: God is particular about the ingredients, and each rule teaches. No leaven — for leaven, which spreads and ferments, is Scripture's picture of corruption and of sin's creeping influence (cf. 1 Cor 5:6-8). No honey — a natural sweetness that ferments and sours, perhaps a warning against worship built on mere pleasant feeling. But always salt: "You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing." Salt preserves; it does not spoil; it was exchanged in the ancient world to seal a binding, lasting agreement — a "covenant of salt" (Num 18:19). So even in a handful of flour, God writes his faithfulness: our fellowship with him is preserved, permanent, incorruptible. The offering that represents our work must be free from the corruption of sin and seasoned with the enduring loyalty of the covenant. Jesus would take up the image and say to his people, "You are the salt of the earth" (Matt 5:13) — "have salt in yourselves" (Mark 9:50).

verseByVerse.quote: If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain. And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with the grain offering of firstfruits — the very first of the new harvest, roasted and crushed, given to God before the rest is enjoyed. To bring the firstfruits is to confess that the whole harvest is God's gift and God's due, and to give him the first and best rather than the leftovers. It is an act of faith as well as thanks: the farmer surrenders the first of the crop trusting that more will follow from the God who gave it. Notice the crushing and the fire — even this thanksgiving gift passes through hard treatment before it rises as a pleasing aroma. And firstfruits always point beyond themselves. Christ is risen as "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees all the rest. To give God the firstfruits is to trust the God who gives the whole.

2.theology:
Consecrated work. The fruit of human labor, offered to God, becomes worship. There is no merely secular work for the believer; all is dedicated to the Lord.

The exclusion of corruption. No leaven, no honey — holiness admits no fermenting agent of sin. Christ alone was utterly unleavened, the sinless bread offered to God.

The covenant of salt. The enduring, incorruptible faithfulness of God's covenant, kept perfectly by Christ and reflected in a people called to be salt.
2.examples:
Then: The Israelite farmer brought the ground fruit of his fields, seasoned with salt, free of leaven — dedicating the produce of his labor to the God who gave the increase.

Now: We offer our work, our wages, our ordinary toil to God as worship. And we look to Christ, the true bread, the grain of wheat that died to bring forth much fruit.

3.title: The Peace Offering: Communion Restored
3.text: <sup>1</sup>If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering... <sup>5</sup>...a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. <sup>16</sup>...All fat is the LORD's. <sup>17</sup>It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood.
3.overview:
The peace offering, the shelamim — from the great word shalom — is the offering of fellowship, of communion, of restored relationship. It is unique among the sacrifices in that the worshipper eats it. After God receives the fat and the priests their portion, the offerer and his household sit down to a sacred meal in the presence of God. This is the only sacrifice that ends in a feast.

Wenham points out that the peace offering celebrates the reconciliation that the other offerings make possible. The burnt offering atones; the peace offering rejoices. Here is the goal of all sacrifice: not merely the removal of guilt but the restoration of communion, table-fellowship with the living God. Sin had banished man from God's presence; the peace offering brings him back to the table.

The fat and the blood belong to God alone — the fat as the richest portion, the choicest part reserved for him, and the blood because it is the life, sacred and not to be consumed. The worshipper learns that even in joyful fellowship, God is God; the best is his.

And Christ is our peace (Eph 2:14). "Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1). The peace offering anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled people of God sit down to eat in his presence, sharing in the body and blood of the one whose sacrifice made peace "by the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). Every Communion is a peace-offering feast — the celebration meal of those brought home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third sacrifice is the peace offering (Hebrew shelamim, from shalom) — the fellowship offering. It is unique in one glad respect: the worshiper shares in it, eating a meal from the sacrifice in the presence of God. The fat and the blood belong wholly to the LORD, but the rest becomes a feast of communion. This is the offering of peace made and enjoyed — reconciliation not only accomplished but celebrated at a shared table.
verseByVerse.theology: The peace offering pictures reconciled fellowship with God — a meal shared in his presence — and so points to "peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1) and to the table of communion he spreads (1 Cor 10:16-18). The fat, the richest part, is burned wholly to God (v.16), and the blood is never eaten (v.17), for "the life... is in the blood" and belongs to God alone (Lev 17:11). The best is God's; yet God invites the worshiper to eat and rejoice in his presence — grace that does not merely pardon but welcomes to the feast.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the reconciled worshiper sat down to eat before the LORD, sharing a joyful meal from his own peace offering — fellowship restored and celebrated.

Now: we who "were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (Eph 2:13), and he is "our peace" (Eph 2:14). At his Table we eat in his presence, no longer enemies but guests — and one day at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD. And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering... Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary: The peace offering, or fellowship offering, is the most joyful of all the sacrifices, because it ends in a shared meal. As with the burnt offering, the worshiper lays his hand on the animal's head, identifying with it, and it is slain and its blood thrown against the altar. But here something different happens: not all of it is burned. This is the one offering the worshiper gets to eat. Think about what that means. Peace with God is not merely the removal of hostility; it is the restoration of fellowship, and fellowship in the Bible is expressed by eating together. To sit at a table and share a meal is to be at peace, to belong, to be welcomed. The peace offering says that God does not merely tolerate the reconciled sinner at a distance; he sits him down to eat in his presence. This is the offering of shalom — wholeness, well-being, reconciliation — and it points straight to the peace we have "with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1), and to the Table where we still eat in his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: All fat is the LORD's... And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary: Though the worshiper shares in the meal, two things are reserved entirely for God: the fat and the blood. The fat — the richest, choicest part — is burned wholly on the altar, for "all fat is the LORD's" (v.16). Here is a principle that runs through all true worship: the best belongs to God. Not the leftovers, not the scraps, but the richest portion is given up to him. Even in the offering the worshiper gets to enjoy, the finest part goes first to God. It is a rebuke to every half-hearted religion that gives God what is left over after self has been satisfied. In the fellowship meal, God is honored first with the best, and only then does the worshiper feast — and the feast is the sweeter for it, because it is enjoyed in the presence of a God who has been given his due.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with a permanent statute: eat neither fat nor blood. The fat is God's portion, as we have seen. But the blood is set apart for a deeper reason, spelled out later: "the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement" (17:11). Blood represents life, and life belongs to God alone; it is not ours to consume, and it is far too sacred to treat as food, for it is the God-given means of atonement. This reverence for blood runs all through Scripture and reaches its fulfillment at the cross, where the blood of Christ, poured out, actually accomplishes what all these sacrifices only pictured — "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22). Even a dietary law, it turns out, was guarding a truth the whole Bible is built on: that life is God's, and atonement comes only through blood given in our place.

3.theology:
Peace with God. The reconciliation accomplished by atonement issues in restored fellowship — the very heart of shalom, fulfilled in Christ "who is our peace" (Eph 2:14).

The fellowship meal. The shared meal anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled feast in God's presence on the body and blood of Christ.

God's claim on the best. The fat belongs to the LORD — God receives the choicest portion, not the leftovers.
3.examples:
Then: An Israelite family, reconciled to God, sat down to a joyful sacred meal in his courts, the fat ascending to God, the meat shared in fellowship and thanksgiving.

Now: At the Lord's Table we celebrate the peace Christ made by his blood. The peace offering teaches us that the gospel's goal is not mere pardon but feasting fellowship with our God.

4.title: The Sin Offering: Even Unintended Sin
4.text: <sup>2</sup>...If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them... <sup>3</sup>if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people... <sup>20</sup>...and the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
4.overview:
Now the tone deepens. The burnt, grain, and peace offerings were largely voluntary expressions of devotion. The sin offering, the chatta't, is mandatory — it deals with the dreadful fact of guilt. And its first and most arresting lesson is this: it is provided for sins committed unintentionally. Sins we never noticed, never meant, never even knew we were committing — these too defile, these too require blood.

Sproul drove this home with terrifying clarity: we so easily measure sin by our intentions, but God measures it by his holiness. The sin offering teaches that guilt is not chiefly a matter of malice but of contamination. Even the sin we stumble into unawares pollutes the sanctuary and bars us from God. If unintentional sin is this serious, what shall we say of the high-handed, deliberate rebellions of our hearts?

The chapter is structured by a striking gradation of rank. The anointed priest, the whole congregation, the leader, the common person — each requires an offering, and the higher the office, the costlier the sacrifice. The priest and the congregation require a bull; the leader a male goat; the common person a female goat or lamb. Leadership carries greater accountability before God.

And here Christ bears the sins of the whole people. He is the sin offering — "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21). The blood of the sin offering was taken into the Holy Place; Christ entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, bearing not the unintentional sins of one man but the mountainous, deliberate sins of a countless multitude. "They shall be forgiven" — the most beautiful refrain in the chapter — is purchased for us at infinite cost.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the sin offering (Hebrew chattath), for sins committed "unintentionally" — the wrongs done in ignorance or weakness, not high-handed rebellion. Even these must be atoned for, because sin is sin whether we meant it or not. The offering is graded by responsibility: the anointed priest and the whole congregation bring a costly bull; a leader brings a male goat; a common person a female goat or lamb. The greater the position, the greater the accountability — but for all alike, blood must be shed and atonement made.
verseByVerse.theology: The sin offering exposes two sobering truths: sin defiles even when unintentional (vv.2, 13, 22, 27), and guilt is graded by responsibility — the priest and congregation, whose sin misleads others, bring the costliest offering (cf. Luke 12:48; James 3:1). The blood applied to the altar (and, for priest and congregation, before the veil) cleanses the sanctuary that sin has polluted. And strikingly, the body of the bull is burned "outside the camp" (vv.11-12) — which Hebrews seizes upon: "Jesus also suffered outside the gate" (Heb 13:11-13), bearing our sin in the place of rejection.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even a sin done in ignorance, once known, drove the worshiper to the altar with a substitute — for unintended sin is still real guilt before a holy God.

Now: we cannot plead "I didn't mean to" before God; but we need not, for Christ, who "suffered outside the gate," has borne even our unknown sins (Ps 19:12; 1 John 1:7). His blood cleanses us from all sin.

verseByVerse.quote: If it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering... And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it... on a fire of wood.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sin offering deals with sins done "unintentionally" — not the defiant, high-handed rebellion, but the wrongs of weakness, ignorance, and inadvertence. And the first case is striking: it begins not with the common man but with "the anointed priest," whose sin "brings guilt on the people." The leader's sin is never merely private; it corrupts those he represents. So he must bring the costliest offering, a bull, and its blood is carried right up to the veil and sprinkled before it, for his sin has polluted the very sanctuary. Then something unusual: the body of the bull is carried "outside the camp" and burned there, in the place of uncleanness and rejection. Centuries later the writer to the Hebrews would fix on that detail: "Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured" (Heb 13:12-13). Our sin-bearer was cast out, crucified beyond the city wall, so that we, the guilty, might be brought in.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally... when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering... Thus the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: Next, the sin of "the whole congregation." A whole community can sin together — drift into a wrong practice, tolerate an evil, share a blindness — and corporate sin is real guilt that corporate atonement must address. The elders lay their hands on the bull's head on behalf of all the people, and its blood is brought before the veil. Then comes one of the sweetest refrains in Leviticus: "and they shall be forgiven." Do not rush past those words in a book so full of blood and ritual. The whole apparatus of sacrifice exists for this — that guilty people might be forgiven. God did not give these laws to crush his people under endless requirement, but to provide a way, again and again, for sin to be dealt with and fellowship restored. And every "they shall be forgiven" in Leviticus rests, finally, on the one sacrifice toward which they all point — the blood of Christ that truly "cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done... he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish... And if anyone of the common people sins unintentionally... he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the leader ("when a leader sins") and then the ordinary Israelite. Notice the grading: the leader brings a male goat, the common person a female goat or lamb — a lesser offering than the priest's or congregation's bull. Responsibility scales the offering. Those who lead, teach, and represent others carry heavier accountability before God, "for everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required" (Luke 12:48; cf. James 3:1). Yet the same truths hold for every rank: sin, even unintended, is real guilt; a spotless substitute must die; blood must be applied; and then — again and again — "he shall be forgiven." From high priest to humblest peasant, there is one road to God, and it runs through the blood of a substitute. No one is too important to need it, and no one is too lowly to receive it. The ground is level at the altar, as it is level at the cross.

4.theology:
The gravity of unintentional sin. Sin defiles whether or not we intend it; guilt is measured by God's holiness, not our awareness. This shatters self-righteousness.

Graded accountability. The higher the office, the costlier the offering — leadership carries greater responsibility before God (cf. James 3:1).

'They shall be forgiven.' The refrain of grace. Christ the sin offering secures the forgiveness the bulls and goats could only foreshadow (2 Cor 5:21; Heb 10:4).
4.examples:
Then: An Israelite, suddenly conscious of a sin he had committed unawares, brought a goat, laid his hand on its head, and heard the priest pronounce him forgiven.

Now: We are guiltier than we know — but in Christ, more loved than we dared hope. The sin offering drives us to the cross, where the deepest, most hidden guilt is fully and finally covered.

5.title: The Guilt Offering: Forgiveness and Restoration
5.text: <sup>5</sup>...when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed... <sup>15</sup>If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD... he shall make restitution... and shall add a fifth to it. <sup>16</sup>...and the priest shall make atonement for him... and he shall be forgiven.
5.overview:
The guilt offering, the 'asham (also called the reparation offering), overlaps with the sin offering but adds a vital dimension: restitution. Where a sin has caused measurable loss — a debt to God's holy things or a fraud against a neighbor — the guilty party must not only bring a sacrifice but make full restitution, adding a fifth. Forgiveness does not float free of repair. Grace does not excuse us from making things right; it empowers us to.

This is the offering that demands confession (5:5) — the open naming of sin before God. And it is the offering that joins atonement to amendment, the altar to the ledger. The reconciled sinner returns the stolen, repays the defrauded, and adds twenty percent on top. Zacchaeus, climbing down from his tree to give back fourfold (Luke 19:8), is a son of the guilt offering, transformed by grace into a maker of restitution.

Wenham observes the moral seriousness here: God cares not only that we feel forgiven but that the web of relationships torn by our sin be rewoven. The guilt offering refuses cheap grace.

And Christ is the One who not only forgives but restores. Isaiah 53:10 says, "when his soul makes an offering for guilt" — the suffering Servant is himself the 'asham. He pays not only the principal of our debt but the added fifth and infinitely more, restoring to God a glory greater than Adam lost, and restoring to us a sonship richer than Eden. He gives back what he never took away (Ps 69:4). The guilt offering points to a Savior who does not merely cancel our debt but rebuilds what sin demolished.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Sin Offering Scaled to the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sin offering continues with specific cases — failing to testify, touching what is unclean, a rash oath — and with a tender provision: if the sinner cannot afford a lamb, he may bring two birds; and if he cannot even afford birds, a little fine flour. God will not let poverty bar anyone from atonement. The way to forgiveness is scaled so that no one is shut out.
verseByVerse.theology: The graded offering (lamb, then birds, then flour, vv.7, 11) proclaims that atonement is accessible to all — God's provision reaches down to the very poorest, so no one is excluded for lack of means. Confession is required (v.5): the sinner must name his sin, not hide it. Even the flourguilt offering still makes atonement "and he shall be forgiven" (v.13) — for the efficacy was never in the value of the gift but in the God who accepts it, and ultimately in the one Sacrifice all these foreshadow.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the poorest Israelite, unable to afford a lamb, could still bring a handful of flour and be forgiven — the door to God open to empty hands.

Now: salvation is "without money and without price" (Isa 55:1). The poorest sinner is welcomed on the same terms as the richest, for the price was paid in full by Christ. Come as you are, with empty hands.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness... yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity... when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed... he shall bring to the LORD... a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here the sin offering addresses specific, everyday failures: staying silent when you should testify, touching something unclean, swearing a rash oath. These are the ordinary sins of ordinary life — and they matter to God. Notice the sequence that leads to forgiveness: "when he realizes his guilt... and confesses the sin he has committed." Atonement is not automatic or mechanical; it requires that the sinner come to see his sin, own it, and name it before God. Confession is the turning point. There is no forgiveness for the sin we will not admit, but there is full forgiveness for the sin we bring honestly to God. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9). The sinner who stops hiding, stops excusing, and simply confesses — that sinner finds a Substitute waiting and atonement made.

verseByVerse.quote: But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD... two turtledoves or two pigeons... And if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring... a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering... and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now watch the tenderness of God. If the sinner cannot afford a lamb, he may bring two birds. And if he is so poor he cannot even manage two birds, he may bring a small measure of fine flour. God bends all the way down to the poorest of the poor, so that no one — no one — is shut out of forgiveness for lack of money. The value of the offering was never the point; the point was a way provided by grace, and that way is open to empty hands. And do not miss the final words, spoken even over a handful of flour: "and he shall be forgiven." The pauper's flour and the rich man's lamb secure the same forgiveness, because the power to forgive was never in the gift but in the God who receives it, and in the one true Sacrifice they all foreshadow. This is the gospel's own generosity: "Come, everyone who thirsts... he who has no money, come, buy and eat!" (Isa 55:1). Salvation is free, and it is for the penniless.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last of the five offerings is the guilt (or trespass) offering (Hebrew asham), for a "breach of faith" — especially sins that defraud God or neighbor of what is owed. It is unique in requiring restitution: the wrong must not only be atoned for by blood but repaid in full, plus a fifth added. Forgiveness and repair go together; grace makes wrongs right.
verseByVerse.theology: The guilt offering joins atonement to restitution: the offender must "make restitution... and add a fifth to it" (v.16). True repentance does more than feel sorry; where possible, it repairs the damage and restores what was taken (cf. Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus). Yet the added blood offering shows that restitution alone cannot cover guilt before God — even a repaid debt leaves a stain that only sacrifice removes. Both are needed, and both are fulfilled in Christ, who is called an asham, a guilt offering, in Isaiah 53:10 ("when his soul makes an offering for guilt").
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the man who defrauded had to bring a ram in atonement and repay what he owed with a fifth added — sin forgiven and wrong repaired.

Now: grace still moves us to make things right: to return, repay, and reconcile where we have wronged others (Matt 5:23-24). And it rests on the true guilt offering, Christ, who made restitution we could never make (Isa 53:10).

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation... a ram without blemish... And he shall make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him... and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final offering is the guilt offering, and it adds a dimension the others do not emphasize: restitution. It deals with a "breach of faith" — sins that rob God or neighbor of what is rightly owed, whether tithes withheld, holy things misused, or a neighbor defrauded (the next chapter extends it to wrongs against people). And here the sinner must do two things: bring a ram in atonement, and repay what he took, plus a fifth on top. Forgiveness and repair travel together. It is not enough to feel sorry and offer a sacrifice while the stolen goods stay in your pocket. Real repentance restores. Zacchaeus understood this when he met Jesus and cried, "if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). Yet notice: the restitution does not replace the blood. Even a fully repaid debt leaves a guilt before God that only sacrifice can cover. Both are needed. And both meet in Christ, whom Isaiah calls a guilt offering — "when his soul makes an offering for guilt" (Isa 53:10) — the one who both atones for our sin and restores what we could never repay.

5.theology:
Confession. Sin must be named openly before God. The guilt offering enshrines confession as the gateway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

Restitution. Grace does not bypass repair; it empowers it. The forgiven make things right, even adding a fifth — repentance overpays.

Christ our restorer. The suffering Servant is himself the guilt offering (Isa 53:10), who does not merely forgive but restores, giving back what he never took away (Ps 69:4).
5.examples:
Then: An Israelite who had defrauded another or robbed God's holy things confessed, repaid the loss with a fifth added, and brought a ram — his repentance bearing fruit in restored relationships.

Now: Real repentance still makes restitution. And we rest in Christ, the guilt offering who not only cancels our debt but rebuilds everything sin destroyed.

6.title: Laws for the Priests: The Fire That Never Goes Out
6.text: <sup>12</sup>The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning... <sup>13</sup>Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
6.overview:
Chapters 6 and 7 turn from the worshipper's instructions to the priests' instructions — the administrative regulations for handling each offering. This may seem the dustiest corner of Leviticus, yet it glows with quiet glory. The God who is a consuming fire orders his worship down to the disposal of ashes, because nothing about approaching him is trivial.

The towering image of chapter 6 is the perpetual fire: "Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out" (6:13). Twice the command is repeated. The flame that first fell from God himself (9:24) was never to be allowed to die. The priests fed it every morning. It burned through the night. It was the visible sign that atonement was always available, that the door to God never closed, that the fire of his presence and the fire of sacrifice burned on, unceasing.

Begg loves to draw the line to the believer's heart: there is a fire that must never go out, a devotion fed morning by morning, a flame of love for God tended daily lest it gutter into cold ash. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). The Reformers spoke of the daily mortification of sin and the daily stoking of grace — the morning wood laid on the altar of the heart.

Above all, the perpetual fire foreshadows the perpetual efficacy of Christ's sacrifice. The altar fire never went out because Israel sinned without ceasing and needed atonement without ceasing. But Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb 10:12). The one offering that need never be repeated has made the endless fire unnecessary — yet the devotion it symbolized burns brighter than ever in hearts set aflame by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Restitution for Sins Against a Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guilt offering now reaches beyond sins against holy things to sins against people — deceiving a neighbor, robbery, oppression, keeping what was found, swearing falsely. And again the pattern: atonement by blood, and restitution in full plus a fifth. Sins against our neighbor are also sins against God, and grace repairs both the guilt and the harm.
verseByVerse.theology: Wronging a neighbor is a "breach of faith against the LORD" (v.2) — every social sin is also a sin against God (cf. Ps 51:4). Genuine repentance restores what was taken, adding a fifth (v.5), before bringing the atoning ram. Vertical forgiveness and horizontal repair belong together (Matt 5:23-24). The order matters: make it right with your neighbor, and find your peace with God — both secured, finally, in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the man who cheated his neighbor had to return the goods with interest and bring a guilt offering — his sin against man confessed as sin against God.

Now: "if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you... first be reconciled" (Matt 5:23-24). Grace makes us restorers, not just penitents.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor... he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it... And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary: The guilt offering now turns from sins against sacred things to sins against people — cheating a neighbor over a deposit, robbery, extortion, keeping lost property and lying about it, swearing falsely. And here is a truth easy to forget: God calls defrauding your neighbor "a breach of faith against the LORD." Every sin against another person is also, and first, a sin against God, for he is the one whose law we break and whose image we assault in our neighbor. David saw it: "Against you, you only, have I sinned" (Ps 51:4). So the remedy has two parts. The offender must make full restitution and add a fifth — actually repairing the harm he did — and he must bring the atoning ram. Repentance that costs the sinner nothing and restores the victim nothing is not the repentance God asks. Grace does not merely make us feel forgiven; it makes us restorers, eager to put right what we have wronged. Jesus said the same: make peace with your brother, and then bring your gift to the altar (Matt 5:23-24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Fire That Never Goes Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives the priests their standing orders, beginning with the burnt offering. The altar fire is to burn all night and never be allowed to die: "The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out." Each morning the priest feeds it fresh wood. The continual fire is a picture of worship and atonement that never ceases — and of a devotion that must be daily tended.
verseByVerse.theology: "Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out" (v.13) — a perpetual fire testifying that atonement and worship never lapse before God. It must be actively tended each morning; holy fire, left unfed, dies down. So Paul urges, "fan into flame the gift of God" (2 Tim 1:6), and "be fervent in spirit" (Rom 12:11). Devotion is not a spark struck once but a fire kept.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: through every dark night the altar fire glowed, and each dawn the priest laid on fresh wood — the flame never permitted to die.

Now: the fire of devotion must be tended, not assumed. Feed it daily — with the Word, with prayer, with worship — lest it smolder to ash. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19).

verseByVerse.quote: The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it... Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's instructions to the priests begin with the burnt offering and a command repeated for emphasis: the fire on the altar must never go out. All night the offering burns; each morning the priest clears the ashes and lays on fresh wood so the flame keeps blazing. "Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out." There is deep instruction here. The altar fire pictures worship and atonement rising to God without a break — God is never left unworshiped, the way to him never closed. But notice that the perpetual fire must be actively tended. It does not keep itself; someone must feed it every single morning, or it dies down to embers. So it is with devotion to God. The fire of love and worship in the heart is not a spark struck once at conversion and left to burn on its own; it must be tended daily, fed with the fuel of the Word, prayer, and obedience, or it smolders and cools. Paul's counsel is pure Leviticus 6: "fan into flame the gift of God" (2 Tim 1:6); "do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). Keep the fire burning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-23 — The Priests and the Grain Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The grain offering laws follow: a handful is burned to God, and the rest the priests eat — but as "most holy," only in the holy place, and unleavened. A special grain offering is prescribed for the day a priest is anointed, wholly burned, none of it eaten. Those who serve at the altar are fed from the altar, yet everything they handle is holy and must be treated as such.
verseByVerse.theology: "The priests who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings" (1 Cor 9:13-14) — God feeds his servants from his own table. Yet the priest's portion is "most holy" (v.17): those who handle holy things must handle them with reverence, never carelessly. The priest's own anointing-day offering is wholly burned, not eaten (v.23) — even the mediator gives himself entirely to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priests ate their portion of the offerings, provided for by God through the worship of the people, yet handled it all as most holy.

Now: those who labor in the gospel are worthy of support (1 Cor 9:14), and all who serve God must handle holy things with holy hands — reverence, not routine.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law of the grain offering... And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place... It is most holy... Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary: The grain offering laws show God providing for his servants: after a handful is burned to God, the priests eat the rest. Those who serve at the altar are fed from the altar — a principle Paul carries straight into the church: "those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel" (1 Cor 9:14). God does not ask his ministers to serve on empty stomachs; he feeds them through the worship of his people. Yet the priest's portion is "most holy," eaten only in a holy place, kept free from leaven. Even the food of the servants is sacred; those who handle holy things must handle them with reverence, never with a shrug. And one telling detail: the grain offering a priest brings on the day of his own anointing is not eaten at all but wholly burned. Even the mediator, at his consecration, gives himself entirely to God, holding nothing back. Those who would feed others from God's altar must first be wholly God's own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sin offering laws close the chapter. It too is "most holy"; whatever its blood touches becomes holy, and the priests eat their portion in the holy place — except when the blood was brought into the sanctuary itself, in which case the offering is wholly burned, not eaten. Holiness clings to these things; sin is dealt with in utmost seriousness and utmost reverence.
verseByVerse.theology: The sin offering is "most holy," and its holiness is contagious — "whatever touches its flesh shall be holy" (v.27). Sin is taken with deadly seriousness, and the means of its removal is treated as sacred. That the priests eat the sin offering (except when its blood entered the sanctuary) even pictures the priest bearing the people's sin (cf. Lev 10:17) — a shadow of the great Priest who truly "bore our sins in his body" (1 Pet 2:24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the sin offering was handled as most holy, its blood and flesh treated with grave reverence — sin's remedy never taken lightly.

Now: we must never grow casual about sin or about the cross that answers it. What cost the blood of Christ should never be treated as common (Heb 10:29).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy... Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy... But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with the law of the sin offering, and one word governs it all: "most holy." Even the animal that carries away sin is treated as sacred — killed in the holy place, its blood handled with care, its flesh so holy that "whatever touches its flesh shall be holy." There is a striking lesson in this. We might expect the sin-bearing offering to be treated as defiled, since it is loaded with the people's guilt. Instead it is "most holy," because it is God's appointed means of cleansing, and everything to do with the removal of sin is sacred to him. God is never casual about sin, and he is never casual about its remedy. The priests eat their portion (bearing the sin, as 10:17 will explain) — unless the blood was carried into the sanctuary itself, in which case the whole is burned. Behind all these careful distinctions stands a single conviction: sin is deadly serious, and the way of atonement is holy ground. How much more, then, should we tremble at the true sin offering, and never treat the blood of Christ as a common thing (Heb 10:29).

6.theology:
The perpetual fire. The unceasing altar flame signified the constant availability of atonement and the constant need of a sinful people — a need answered once for all in Christ (Heb 10:12).

Daily devotion. The morning wood on the altar pictures the discipline of tending the heart's fire lest it grow cold. 'Do not quench the Spirit' (1 Thess 5:19).

Provision for ministers. Those who serve at the altar share in the altar; God provides for his servants through the offerings of his people.
6.examples:
Then: Before dawn the priest stirred the embers, laid on fresh wood, and removed the night's ashes — guarding the flame God himself had kindled so that it never died.

Now: We tend the fire of devotion daily by the Word, prayer, and the Spirit. And we rest in the finished sacrifice that ended the need for endless offerings, even as our hearts burn within us (Luke 24:32).

7.title: The Portion of the Priests: Order in Holy Things
7.text: <sup>11</sup>And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD... <sup>26</sup>You shall not eat any blood whatever, whether of bird or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. <sup>34</sup>...I have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 completes the priestly handbook, covering the guilt offering, the peace offering, and the assignment of the priests' portions. To modern ears these are dry logistics; to the eye of faith they reveal the beauty of God's ordered worship. "God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33). The meticulous care given to who eats what, when, and how, teaches that the worship of a holy God is never careless or improvised.

The peace offering is here divided into thanksgiving, vow, and freewill varieties (7:12–16), with the thanksgiving offering to be eaten the same day — joy is not to be hoarded but shared while it is fresh. The breast and the right thigh are assigned to the priests as their "wave offering" and "contribution" (7:30–34), God's gracious provision for those who serve.

Twice more the prohibition of blood and fat is pressed (7:22–27). The blood belongs to God because the life is in it; to eat blood is to seize what is sacred to the Lord alone. This single principle — that blood is life and life is God's — will become the explicit theology of chapter 17 and the foundation of all that Hebrews says about the blood of Christ.

The whole chapter exalts the orderliness of grace. Carson reminds us that the God who saves is the God who orders; redemption is not chaos but the careful, costly, beautiful arrangement of holy things. And every portion reserved, every drop of blood withheld, every wave of the priest's hands points to the day when the perfect Priest would offer the perfect sacrifice and assign to his people the choicest portion of all — himself, the bread and the cup of the new covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Guilt Offering and the Priests' Portions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guilt offering laws are given to the priests, along with a clear provision: the priest who makes atonement receives the hide and the meat as his portion. Those who minister the sacrifices are sustained by them. God ties the servant's provision to his service.
verseByVerse.theology: The priest who ministers the offering is fed by it (vv.6-10) — the enduring principle that "the laborer deserves his wages" (1 Tim 5:18; 1 Cor 9:13-14). God's servants are provided for through the worship they lead, not by their own striving. The guilt offering, "most holy," again ties the seriousness of sin to the sacredness of its remedy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priest received his portion from the very offering he presented — serving God and being sustained by God in one act.

Now: those who devote themselves to God's work should be supported in it (1 Cor 9:14), and all of us serve a God who provides for those who give themselves to him.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy... The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it. And the priest who offers any man's burnt offering shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering that he has offered.
verseByVerse.commentary: The law of the guilt offering is spelled out for the priests, and with it a practical provision: the priest who makes atonement keeps the hide and the meat as his portion. It is the same principle we met in the grain offering — those who minister at the altar are sustained by the altar. God weaves the provision of his servants right into the fabric of worship, so that the priest serving all day at the altar is not left to fend for himself. Paul draws the line straight from here to the church: "Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple... In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel" (1 Cor 9:13-14). And once more the offering is called "most holy," for even in the details of who eats what, the removal of sin is treated as sacred ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-21 — The Peace Offering: Thanksgiving and Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the joyful peace offering, in three kinds: thanksgiving, a vow, or a freewill offering. The thanksgiving offering must be eaten the same day — gratitude is not to be hoarded but enjoyed at once. And strict warnings guard the meal: the unclean may not share in it. Fellowship with God is a feast, but a holy feast, not to be treated carelessly.
verseByVerse.theology: The thank offering (todah) eaten the same day (v.15) teaches that gratitude is to be expressed promptly and gladly, not stored up or delayed. The peace offering is the offering of joy and communion (cf. Ps 116:17, "the sacrifice of thanksgiving"). Yet the warnings against eating it unclean (vv.20-21) show that fellowship with a holy God, though joyful, is never casual — we come to the Table with reverence (1 Cor 11:27-29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the grateful worshiper feasted that very day on his thank offering, sharing the joy with family and friends in God's presence.

Now: gratitude is meant to be expressed, not postponed. "Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving" (Ps 50:14) — and come to his Table with joy and reverence together.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD. If he offers it for a thanksgiving... And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
verseByVerse.commentary: The peace offering is the offering of joy, and it comes in three flavors: thanksgiving, the payment of a vow, or a spontaneous freewill gift. Look at the rule for the thanksgiving offering: it must be eaten the same day, with nothing left till morning. Why the hurry? Because gratitude is meant to be poured out at once, freely and gladly, not carefully rationed or put off. A thankful heart feasts today. It gathers family and friends to share the meal in God's presence and celebrate his goodness while the mercy is fresh. There is a lesson here for slow and stingy hearts: when God has been good to you, say so, and say so now — "offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving" (Ps 50:14). Yet the chapter also fences the feast with warnings: no one unclean may share in it. The peace offering is joyful, but it is holy joy. Fellowship with God is a feast, not a free-for-all; we come to his table glad, but also reverent (cf. 1 Cor 11:27-29).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A solemn prohibition is repeated: eat no fat and no blood. The fat is the LORD's, the choicest part reserved for him; the blood is the life, sacred as the means of atonement. To break this is to be "cut off" from the people. God's people are marked even by how they eat.
verseByVerse.theology: The double prohibition guards two truths: the best (the fat) belongs to God, and life (the blood) is his alone and is the appointed means of atonement (17:11). The severity — "cut off" (v.27) — underscores how sacred blood is. It all magnifies the blood of Christ, poured out to secure what these laws protected in shadow (Heb 9:22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel honored God even at the dinner table, giving him the fat and reverencing the blood as sacred.

Now: the reverence for blood points us to the cross, where the lifeblood of Christ was poured out for us. We treat that blood as holy, never common (Heb 10:29).

verseByVerse.quote: You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat... You shall eat no blood whatever, whether of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. Whoever eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.commentary: The prohibition on fat and blood is repeated with force. The fat, as we have seen, is God's portion — the richest part, given first to him. But the ban on blood carries a weight all its own, and breaking it means being "cut off from his people." Why so serious? Because, as God will explain, "the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement" (17:11). Blood stands for life, and life belongs to God alone; it is not ours to consume, and it is far too sacred to treat as ordinary food, because it is the very thing by which sin is atoned. Even at the dinner table, God was teaching his people a truth the whole Bible would build upon: forgiveness comes only through lifeblood poured out. Every drop reverenced in Leviticus points forward to the blood of Christ, shed for us, apart from which "there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22). What God guarded so carefully in the law, he poured out so freely at the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes by assigning the priests their portions of the peace offerings — the breast, waved before the LORD, and the right thigh, contributed to the officiating priest. So Aaron and his sons are provided for "as a perpetual due." The section that began with the offerings ends with God's faithful provision for those who serve.
verseByVerse.theology: The wave breast and the contributed thigh (vv.30-34) are given to the priests as "a perpetual due" — God's ongoing provision for his ministers, woven into the worship itself. The whole block of offering laws (chs 1-7) ends here (v.37-38), a complete manual of approach to God, given at Sinai — and all of it a shadow of "good things to come" in Christ (Heb 10:1).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priests received the breast and thigh as their steady portion, provided for by God through the people's worship, generation after generation.

Now: God still provides for those who give their lives to his service, and the whole sacrificial system he here completes points us to the one perfect Sacrifice (Heb 10:1, 12).

verseByVerse.quote: The breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'... the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings... This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings... This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, and of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering.
verseByVerse.commentary: The offering laws end where they must — with God faithfully providing for his servants. The breast of the peace offering, waved before the LORD, and the right thigh, contributed to the officiating priest, become the portion of Aaron and his sons "as a perpetual due." Once more we see that those who serve at the altar are fed from the altar, generation after generation, by God's own arrangement. Then comes a summary line that gathers up the whole first section of Leviticus: "This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering... and of the peace offering." Seven chapters, five offerings, one grand subject: how sinful people may draw near to a holy God. Burnt offering (total consecration), grain offering (thankful dedication of labor), peace offering (restored fellowship), sin offering (cleansing from defilement), guilt offering (restitution and atonement) — together they are a complete picture of what it costs to come to God, and a complete portrait, in shadow, of the One who would fulfill them all. "These are but a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Col 2:17; cf. Heb 10:1).

7.theology:
The order of worship. God's meticulous regulation of holy things reflects that he is 'not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor 14:33). Redemption is ordered, not chaotic.

The sanctity of blood. The life is in the blood, and the blood belongs to God — the foundation of atonement theology fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. The todah offering becomes, in Christ, the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
7.examples:
Then: The reconciled Israelite shared a thanksgiving feast the same day, the priests received the breast and thigh, and not a drop of blood was consumed — every detail ordered by God.

Now: We offer the sacrifice of praise through Christ, support those who serve God's people, and marvel that the blood once forbidden is now, in Christ, the cup of salvation.

8.title: The Ordination of Aaron: Consecrated by Blood and Oil
8.text: <sup>12</sup>And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him. <sup>23</sup>...and Moses... put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. <sup>30</sup>...and consecrated Aaron and his garments...
8.overview:
From the laws of sacrifice we turn to the consecration of those who will administer them. Chapters 8–10 form the great narrative center of the offering section: the ordination of Aaron and his sons, their first ministry, and the catastrophe that follows. Chapter 8 is the seven-day investiture of the priesthood, carried out by Moses, who here acts as the presiding priest, mediating the very mediators.

The ritual is rich with gospel symbol. Aaron is washed with water (8:6) — the cleansing every minister of God needs. He is clothed in the glorious garments (8:7–9), arrayed not in his own righteousness but in robes provided. He is anointed with oil (8:12), set apart by the Spirit's symbol. And he is marked with blood on the ear, the thumb, and the toe (8:23) — the whole man, hearing, working, walking, consecrated to God by sacrifice.

Wenham notes the sevenfold sprinkling and the seven days of waiting (8:33–35): the number of completeness, the patient setting-apart of those who would draw near to God. Aaron could not appoint himself; he was called, washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. "No one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was" (Heb 5:4).

And all of it anticipates Christ's consecration. At his baptism the sinless Son went down into the water, and the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father spoke — the true Aaron washed and anointed for his priestly work (Matt 3:16–17; Acts 10:38). Yet how the contrast dazzles: Aaron needed blood applied to himself for his own sin; Christ needed no cleansing, but became himself the blood of consecration. He is at once the Priest who is anointed and the sacrifice whose blood consecrates. The ear that perfectly heard the Father, the hands that only did good, the feet that never strayed — wholly consecrated, he ordains us "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God commanded in Exodus 29 now actually happens. Moses gathers the whole congregation and, before their eyes, ordains Aaron and his sons: he washes them with water, clothes Aaron in the glorious garments, and pours the anointing oil on his head. The priests are publicly, visibly made ready to stand between God and the people. The pattern is the pattern of every servant God calls: cleansed, clothed, anointed.
verseByVerse.theology: The ordination is done publicly, "before the congregation" (v.5) — the priesthood is a public trust, not a private honor. Washed (cleansing, Titus 3:5), clothed (imputed righteousness, Isa 61:10), anointed (the Spirit, 1 John 2:20): the same threefold pattern by which God fits any servant for his service, fulfilled in Christ the Anointed and extended to his royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:9; Rev 1:6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the people watched their priests washed, robed, and anointed — made ready by God's own prescribed means to draw near on their behalf.

Now: you were "washed... sanctified... justified" (1 Cor 6:11) and anointed by the Spirit, made "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6). What Aaron received, all God's people share in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to the congregation, 'This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done.'... And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water... And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him, to consecrate him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The blueprint of Exodus 29 now becomes reality. Moses assembles the whole congregation — for the making of priests is a public act, not a private ceremony — and step by step he ordains Aaron and his sons exactly as God commanded. First he washes them with water: no one serves God uncleansed. Then he clothes Aaron in the holy garments, the ephod and breastpiece and golden plate, glory and beauty draped over a sinful man. Then he pours the anointing oil on Aaron's head, running down (Ps 133:2), setting him apart by the sign of the Spirit. Washed, clothed, anointed — it is the unchanging pattern by which God fits any servant for his service. We do not qualify ourselves; God cleanses us, clothes us in a righteousness not our own, and anoints us by his Spirit. And every drop of that oil points to the great Anointed One, the Christ, through whom all his people are now made "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6). What Israel watched happen to Aaron, God has done for everyone who is in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-21 — The Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the priests, before they can serve, must be atoned for. Moses offers the bull as a sin offering, Aaron and his sons laying their hands on its head, and then the ram as a burnt offering, wholly consumed. The men who will bring others to God must first be brought to God themselves, by blood and by total consecration.
verseByVerse.theology: The priests' own sin offering exposes the weakness of the old order: they must be atoned for before they can atone for others (Heb 5:3; 7:27). The hand laid on the head (vv.14, 18) is substitution; the burnt offering wholly burned is total consecration. All of it magnifies the sinless Priest who needed no sacrifice for himself and became the sacrifice for us (Heb 7:26-27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the new priests laid their hands on the substitute, confessing that they too were sinners who could serve only through atonement.

Now: we come through a High Priest who needed no atoning for himself — "holy, innocent, unstained" (Heb 7:26) — and who is himself the once-for-all offering. Our whole life becomes a burnt offering in response (Rom 12:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering... He presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram... It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the priests can ever bring a sinner to God, they must themselves be brought to God — and that means blood. Moses offers the bull as a sin offering, and Aaron and his sons press their hands on its head, confessing their own guilt and transferring it to the substitute. Then the ram, wholly burned as a burnt offering, a pleasing aroma, a picture of a life given entirely to God. Do not miss how humbling this is. The men about to be clothed in glory and set apart as mediators are, first of all, sinners who need atoning for. The old priesthood carried this weakness in its very bones: every priest had to "offer sacrifice... for his own sins" before he could serve others (Heb 5:3). And that is exactly what makes our great High Priest so glorious. He was "holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners" (Heb 7:26); he needed no bull for his own guilt, because he had none. Instead he became the offering itself, once for all (Heb 7:27). Aaron had to be atoned for before he could serve; Christ, needing no atonement, became our atonement.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ram of ordination is offered, and its blood is applied to each priest's right ear, right thumb, and right big toe — what he hears, what he does, where he walks, all claimed by God. Blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on Aaron and his garments. The whole man, and all he will do, is consecrated to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Blood on ear, thumb, and toe (vv.23-24) consecrates the whole person — hearing, working, walking — to God; redemption claims all of us (Rom 6:13; 12:1). The blood and oil together (v.30) join atonement and the Spirit's consecration, the two gifts by which anyone is set apart for God. Nothing of the priest is left to himself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: blood touched the priest's ear, hand, and foot — a vivid sign that no part of him remained his own.

Now: the blood of Christ claims your whole life — your ears for his truth, your hands for his work, your feet for his ways (1 Cor 6:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination... and Moses... put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot... And Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the ram of ordination, and the vivid moment we saw commanded in Exodus 29 actually takes place: Moses dabs its blood on the tip of each priest's right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot.
