Recall what those three parts mean. The ear — what he listens to. The hand — what he does. The foot — where he walks. Blood on all three declares that the priest's hearing, working, and going now belong wholly to God; not one part of him is left as his own. Then Moses sprinkles both blood and anointing oil on Aaron and his garments — atonement and the Spirit together, the two great gifts by which anyone is set apart for God. This is what consecration means: the whole person claimed, redeemed, and given over to the Lord. And it is what the blood of Christ still does for us. Having been "bought with a price," we "present [our] members to God" (1 Cor 6:20; Rom 6:13) — ears, hands, feet, all of it — no longer our own, but his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-36 — Seven Days at the Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ordination is not over in a day. Aaron and his sons must remain at the entrance of the tent of meeting seven days and nights, keeping the LORD's charge, until the consecration is complete. Holiness is thorough and patient; the priests wait a full week at the threshold before they begin to serve.
verseByVerse.theology: Seven days at the door (vv.33-35), keeping "the charge of the LORD, so that you do not die," teaches that consecration is thorough and unhurried, and that access to God is on his terms alone. Obedience "as the LORD commanded" (v.36) frames the whole account. The patient waiting before service warns against presumption and prepares the heart to minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: for seven days the priests stayed at the tent door, waiting, keeping God's charge, before they dared to serve.

Now: God still prepares his servants before he uses them, and still calls us to draw near on his terms, not our own. Faithful service begins with patient obedience at the threshold.

verseByVerse.quote: At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die... And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary: The making of a priest is not the work of an hour. Aaron and his sons must stay at the entrance of the tent, day and night, for seven full days, keeping the LORD's charge until their consecration is complete. Seven days — the number of completeness — and a solemn warning attached: "so that you do not die." Even the newly ordained priests must draw near strictly on God's terms, with reverence, not presumption. There is wisdom here for everyone God calls to serve him. Holiness is thorough and patient; God prepares his servants before he uses them, and a week at the threshold guards against rushing carelessly into holy things. The account closes with the sentence that has governed it all: "Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses." Everything done God's way, in God's order, at God's pace. Tomorrow — the eighth day — the priests will begin their ministry, and the glory of the LORD will appear.

8.theology:
Priesthood conferred from outside. Aaron is washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. No one takes this honor for himself (Heb 5:4); so we are made priests by grace.

Whole-life consecration. Blood on ear, hand, and foot claims the entire person for God — fulfilled as Christ consecrates every faculty of those he saves.

The anointing of the Spirit. The oil poured on Aaron foreshadows the Spirit who anointed Christ at his baptism and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20; Acts 10:38).
8.examples:
Then: For seven days Moses washed, robed, anointed, and blooded Aaron and his sons, setting apart Israel's priesthood with patient, fearful reverence.

Now: Christ, washed and anointed at his baptism, is our consecrated High Priest, and by his blood and Spirit he makes us 'a royal priesthood' (1 Pet 2:9), our whole lives set apart for God.

9.title: The Glory Appears: Fire from Heaven
9.text: <sup>6</sup>And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." <sup>23</sup>...and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. <sup>24</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering... and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
9.overview:
The seven days of preparation are over; the eighth day dawns. Aaron, newly consecrated, offers his first sacrifices — first for himself, then for the people. The whole drama drives toward a single promised climax: "that the glory of the LORD may appear to you" (9:6). All the offerings, all the blood, all the careful ritual aim at this — that sinners might behold the glory of God and live.

And the glory comes. When Aaron and Moses bless the people, "the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people" (9:23). Then fire — the holy fire of God's own presence — flashes out and consumes the offering on the altar. This is heaven's amen, God's visible acceptance of the sacrifice, the divine seal upon the whole sacrificial system. The God who is a consuming fire consumes the substitute and spares the people.

The response is the only fitting one: "when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces" (9:24). Joy and awe, ecstasy and prostration, together. This is worship in the presence of glory — not the casual familiarity of a trifling age but the trembling, exultant adoration of those who have seen the fire fall and lived. Sproul often said that the proper response to the holiness of God is to fall on our faces; here Israel does exactly that, even as they shout for joy.

The fire that fell on the altar fell, at the last, on Christ. At Calvary the consuming fire of God's holiness fell upon the true sacrifice, and he was wholly consumed in our place. And because the fire fell on him, it need never fall on us. The glory that Israel glimpsed for a moment now shines "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), and we who behold it are summoned to the same response: shouting joy and prostrate awe before the God who accepts us in his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-24 — The Glory Appears, and the Fire Falls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is the eighth day. Everything is ready, and Moses tells Aaron why they have labored so: "today the LORD will appear to you." Aaron offers the sin offering and burnt offering for himself, then the offerings for the people, and blesses them. And then it happens: "the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering." The people shout and fall on their faces. God has accepted the sacrifice, and come to dwell — with fire.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole point of the priesthood, the offerings, and the tabernacle is here: "today the LORD will appear to you" (v.4, 6). Atonement leads to appearing — God comes to dwell with a people whose sin has been covered. The fire from the LORD that consumes the offering (v.24) is divine acceptance, God receiving the sacrifice himself (cf. 1 Kgs 18:38; 2 Chr 7:1). It points to the cross, where the fire of God's judgment fell on the true offering, and to the Spirit's fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), God accepting and indwelling his people. The right response to the appearing glory is worship: they "shouted and fell on their faces" (v.24).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: after days of blood and obedience, God answered with fire and glory, accepting the offering before all the people — and they fell on their faces in awe and joy.

Now: the fire of judgment fell on Christ, our offering, and was satisfied; and the fire of the Spirit fell on the church (Acts 2). God has appeared to us "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), and worship is the only fitting response.

verseByVerse.quote: On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel... 'Today the LORD will appear to you.'... And Moses said, 'This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The eighth day dawns, and Aaron begins his ministry. But before a single animal is offered, Moses tells the people why all of this matters, why the tabernacle was built and the priests ordained and the offerings prescribed: "Today the LORD will appear to you." There it is — the goal of everything. All the blood and ritual and careful obedience are not ends in themselves; they are the God-given way to one glorious end: that God might appear and dwell among his people. Notice too the order. First Aaron must offer a sin offering and burnt offering for himself, then for the people — atonement comes before the appearing. God does not show his glory to the unatoned; the way to his presence runs through the altar. This is the pattern of the whole Bible and the whole gospel: sin dealt with, and then — only then — God drawing near. Do the thing God has commanded, Moses says, "that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." Obedience and atonement, and then the glory comes.

verseByVerse.quote: So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself... Then he offered the people's offering... And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule.
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron does it all in careful order — his own sin offering and burnt offering first, then the people's sin offering, burnt offering, grain offering, and peace offerings. Every sacrifice we have studied in the opening chapters of Leviticus is now actually offered, in sequence, by the newly ordained high priest. There is something moving about seeing the theory become practice: the laws of atonement worked out in real blood, real fire, real obedience, on the first day of Israel's ordered worship. And it is all done "according to the rule," exactly as God commanded. This is the shape of true worship — not improvised to human taste, but offered as God directed, through the appointed mediator, on the ground of atoning blood. Aaron draws near for the people because they cannot draw near themselves. He is a shadow of the great High Priest who would draw near for us, offering not the blood of calves and goats but himself, and opening the way for us to come near in him (Heb 9:11-12).

verseByVerse.quote: And Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them... And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering... and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.commentary: And now the promise is kept. Aaron lifts his hands and blesses the people; Moses and Aaron come out of the tent and bless them again; and "the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people." Then the climax: "fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering." God himself sends fire from his presence to devour the sacrifice — visible, unmistakable proof that the offering is accepted, the atonement received, the worship pleasing. This is God saying yes. The same divine fire would fall on Elijah's altar (1 Kgs 18:38) and at the dedication of Solomon's temple (2 Chr 7:1), and it points two ways at once. It points to the cross, where the fire of God's judgment fell not on us but on the true burnt offering, Christ, and was satisfied. And it points to Pentecost, where the fire of God's Spirit fell on the church (Acts 2:3), God accepting and now indwelling his people. What is the right response when the glory appears and the fire falls? The people show us: they "shouted and fell on their faces." Awe and joy together — worship. When you grasp that God has accepted the offering in your place, you will shout, and you will fall down.

9.theology:
The goal of worship: glory. All the offerings aim at the appearing of God's glory (9:6, 23), now seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 4:6).

Divine acceptance. The fire from heaven seals God's acceptance of the sacrifice; the fire that fell on the altar fell ultimately on Christ, so it need never fall on us.

Worship in the presence of glory. Shouting joy and prostrate awe together — the fitting response of redeemed sinners who behold God's glory and live.
9.examples:
Then: Israel watched fire flash from God's presence to consume the offering, and the whole nation shouted and fell prostrate — joy and trembling fused in the sight of glory.

Now: Because the fire of judgment fell on Christ, we behold God's glory not in terror but in worship. The right response to grace is still to shout for joy and fall on our faces.

10.title: Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized Fire
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. <sup>2</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. <sup>3</sup>..."Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified."
10.overview:
The same fire that fell in blessing now falls in judgment. Before the smoke of acceptance has cleared, the joy of chapter 9 is shattered. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's own sons, just consecrated to the priesthood, take their censers and offer "unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them" (10:1). And the holy fire that consumed the sacrifice now consumes the priests. They die before the LORD.

This is the most sobering passage in Leviticus, and Sproul's The Holiness of God circles back to it again and again. We instinctively recoil — was the punishment not severe? But Sproul presses us: our shock reveals how little we grasp the holiness of God and how much we presume upon his grace. The wonder is not that Nadab and Abihu died, but that we live. The fire of judgment is the default reality for sinful creatures who approach a holy God on their own terms.

The exact nature of their sin is debated — strange fire not taken from the altar, presumption, perhaps drunkenness (note the prohibition that follows in v. 9). But the heart of it is clear: they approached God in a way "he had not commanded." They presumed to worship on their own terms. And God's verdict is unbending: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified" (10:3). The closer one draws to God, the more his holiness must be honored. Privilege heightens accountability.

How desperately this drives us to Christ. We too have offered unauthorized fire — worship of our own devising, approach on our own terms, presumption upon grace. We have all deserved the fire. But Christ stepped into the place of judgment; the consuming fire fell on him at Calvary. He is the only authorized way to the Father (John 14:6), the new and living way opened through his flesh (Heb 10:20). Nadab and Abihu teach us, with terrible clarity, that there is no casual coming to God — and that the way which is open is open only because Another bore the fire we earned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The joy of the eighth day turns, in an instant, to horror. Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu take their censers and offer "unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them." And fire — the same fire that had just consumed the sacrifice in acceptance — now comes out from the LORD and consumes them. Moses speaks the terrible lesson: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified." And Aaron, bereaved in the moment of his greatest honor, "held his peace."
verseByVerse.theology: The same fire that signaled acceptance (9:24) now brings judgment (10:2) — God is not to be approached carelessly, even by priests, even in worship. "Unauthorized fire... which he had not commanded" (v.1) is worship on human terms rather than God's; the nearer one stands to God, the more his holiness must be honored: "I will be sanctified... I will be glorified" (v.3; cf. 1 Pet 4:17). This is the sober counterweight to the gospel's boldness: we come freely, but to a God who is "a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), and reverence is never optional. Aaron's silence (v.3) is faith submitting to God's righteous holiness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: in the glow of Israel's happiest day, two priests worshiped on their own terms and were struck dead — and their father bowed in silent submission to a holy God.

Now: we "offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire" (Heb 12:28-29). Grace makes us bold, never casual. God is to be worshiped as he commands, not as we prefer.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer, and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. Then Moses said to Aaron, 'This is what the LORD has said: Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.' And Aaron held his peace.
verseByVerse.commentary: The happiest day becomes the most terrible. Only moments after fire fell from God to consume the sacrifice in acceptance, Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's own sons, offer "unauthorized fire... which he had not commanded them" — worship of their own devising, on their own terms, perhaps in careless presumption. And the same fire that had blessed now kills: it comes out from the LORD and consumes them where they stand. It is a passage that stops us cold, and it is meant to. Moses explains it in words that tremble: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified." The nearer a person stands to God — and no one stood nearer than these priests — the more seriously God's holiness must be honored. God will not be approached carelessly, treated as common, worshiped however we please. This is the sober counterweight to all the grace of Leviticus. Yes, God has flung open a way to himself; but he is still the God who is "a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), and we come with reverence and awe, not casual familiarity. And then, most movingly of all: "Aaron held his peace." No protest, no bitter word. In the crushing loss of his two sons, in the very hour of his triumph, Aaron is silent — faith bowing before the righteous holiness of God, saying with his silence what Job said with his words: "the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-11 — Distinguish the Holy from the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks directly to Aaron with a command that may hint at what went wrong: the priests are not to drink wine or strong drink when they go into the tent, on pain of death. Clear-headed, they must be able "to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean," and to teach Israel all God's statutes. The priest's calling is discernment — and discernment requires sobriety.
verseByVerse.theology: The priests must "distinguish between the holy and the common" (v.10) — the very heart of the priestly vocation, and the heart of Leviticus itself. Sobriety guards that discernment; strong drink blurs the very lines God calls his servants to keep sharp. And they must teach the people (v.11) — truth clearly distinguished and faithfully passed on. The loss of these distinctions is the loss of holiness (cf. Ezek 22:26); recovering them is the work of God's word (Heb 5:14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priest had to keep a clear head, able to tell holy from common and to teach it — sobriety in the service of discernment.

Now: we are called to "discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil" (Heb 5:14), and to sober-minded clarity in a world that blurs every line (1 Pet 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying, 'Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die... You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean, and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Immediately after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, God speaks to Aaron with a pointed command: no wine or strong drink before entering the tent. The timing suggests the warning may be connected to what had just happened — careless, perhaps intoxicated, worship. But the reason God gives opens up the whole calling of the priest: they must be clear-headed "to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean," and "to teach the people" all of God's statutes. Here is the priest's essential work, and indeed the pulse of the entire book of Leviticus: to know the difference between the holy and the common, and to help God's people see it. A drunken priest cannot tell holy from profane; strong drink blurs exactly the lines God calls his servants to keep razor-sharp. And what the priest discerns, he must teach. When these distinctions are lost, holiness itself is lost (Ezek 22:26). The recovery of them — learning to see as God sees, to call holy what he calls holy — is still the work of God's word in his people, training us "to distinguish good from evil" (Heb 5:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-20 — Grief and Grace at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses instructs Aaron and his surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, to eat their portion of the offerings as commanded. But then Moses discovers that the goat of the sin offering was burned, not eaten, and he is angry. Aaron answers with a tender, honest word: after all that had befallen him that day, "would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?" And Moses is satisfied. Even in the strictness of the law, there is room for a grieving heart, and grace understands.
verseByVerse.theology: Aaron's honest reply — that given the day's tragedy, eating the sin offering may not have been fitting — and Moses' acceptance of it (v.20) show that God's law is not a heartless machine. There is a place for grief, for conscience, for pastoral wisdom within obedience. God "knows our frame" (Ps 103:14) and does not crush the bruised reed (Isa 42:3). Holiness and compassion are not enemies; the same God who sent fire on presumption honors the honest heart of a bereaved father.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Aaron, still reeling from the loss of his sons, could not bring himself to eat the sin offering, and God did not condemn his grief — Moses was satisfied.

Now: the God who calls us to obedience also "knows our frame" and meets us tenderly in our sorrow (Ps 103:13-14). Reverence and grief can live together before a compassionate God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar... And Aaron said to Moses, 'Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?' And when Moses heard that, he approved.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends with a scene of surprising tenderness. Moses instructs Aaron and his two surviving sons to eat their portion of the offerings as the law required. But then he finds that the goat of the sin offering has been burned up rather than eaten, and he is angry — the command was not kept to the letter. Aaron answers not with excuses but with the raw honesty of a grieving father: on this day, of all days, with his two sons struck dead, how could he sit down and eat the sin offering as if nothing had happened? "Would it have been acceptable in the sight of the LORD?" And here is the beautiful thing: "when Moses heard that, he approved." The strict law bends to make room for a broken heart. This tells us something precious about the God of Leviticus. He is holy, yes — so holy that presumption brought fire — but he is not a heartless machine of rules. There is room in his law for grief, for conscience, for a shepherd's wisdom. The God who "knows our frame" and "remembers that we are dust" (Ps 103:14) does not crush the bruised reed (Isa 42:3). On one day, and in one man, we see both the fire of God's holiness and the tenderness of his compassion — and they are not at war.

10.theology:
The holiness of God. Sproul's great theme: God must be approached on his terms, not ours. The fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu reveals the deadly seriousness of presumptuous worship.

Privilege heightens accountability. 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified' (10:3) — the closer one is brought to God, the more his holiness must be honored.

The only authorized way. There is one acceptable approach to the Father, and it is Christ (John 14:6); the fire we deserved fell on him.
10.examples:
Then: Aaron's sons offered worship of their own devising and were consumed by holy fire; their father stood in silent, submissive grief before the holiness of God.

Now: We are warned against casual, self-styled worship and driven to Christ, the only authorized way to God, who bore in his own body the fire of judgment we deserved.

11.title: Clean and Unclean: A People Set Apart
11.text: <sup>44</sup>For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy... <sup>45</sup>For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
11.overview:
Now begins the section on clean and unclean (chs 11–15), opening with the dietary laws. Which animals may Israel eat, and which not? On the surface these seem arbitrary; in reality they are a daily, table-level catechism in the great theme of separation. Three times a day, at every meal, Israel was reminded that they were a people set apart, that distinctions matter, that the holy and the common are not the same.

Wenham's classic study shows that the categories are not finally about hygiene but about symbolism: the animals that conform to the created order of their domain are clean; the anomalous, the boundary-crossing, the predatory and death-associated are unclean. The clean animal is a living parable of the people who keep within God's appointed bounds. Every meal preached: be distinct, be whole, be set apart unto God.

And the climax of the chapter is the towering refrain that will dominate the rest of Leviticus: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). The dietary laws are not ends in themselves; they serve this. God grounds the call in redemption — "I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (11:45). Holiness is the grateful response of a redeemed people to their redeeming God.

In Christ, the dietary distinctions are fulfilled and lifted. Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), and Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10) abolishes the wall between clean and unclean nations: "What God has made clean, do not call common." The deeper purpose endures — God still calls his people to be holy and distinct — but the boundary now runs not between Jew and Gentile, kosher and non-kosher, but between those who are in Christ and those who are not. Peter himself quotes Leviticus to the church: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet 1:16). The table-level lesson becomes a life-level call.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God now teaches Israel to distinguish clean animals from unclean — which may be eaten and which may not, among the beasts of the land, the creatures of the water, and the birds and insects of the air. The point is not that some creatures are evil (God made them all), but that Israel is to be a people set apart, reminded at every meal, three times a day, that they belong to a holy God and are different from the nations around them.
verseByVerse.theology: The food laws made holiness a daily, tangible reality — every meal a reminder that Israel was "separated... from the peoples" to be God's own (v.45; 20:26). They taught the great Levitical distinction between clean and unclean, holy and common. These laws were never permanent moral absolutes; Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), and God taught Peter in a vision that the wall was down (Acts 10:15). What endures is the lesson beneath them: God's people are to be distinct, consecrated, visibly his in the ordinary rhythms of life (1 Pet 1:14-16).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: at every meal an Israelite was reminded, by what he could and could not eat, that he belonged to a holy God and was not like the nations.

Now: the dividing wall of food laws is gone in Christ (Mark 7:19; Acts 10), but the call remains: "as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct" (1 Pet 1:15) — distinct not in diet now, but in life.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat... The pig, because it parts the hoof... but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God begins with the land animals, giving Israel signs to tell clean from unclean — the split hoof and the chewing of the cud. We should be careful here: the pig and the camel are not evil creatures, and nothing is wrong with them in themselves; God made them all and called his creation good. The purpose of these laws is not hygiene or morality but holiness in the sense of separateness. Israel was to be a distinct people, and God chose to teach that distinctness through the most ordinary and constant activity of life — eating. Three times a day, at every meal, an Israelite was reminded: you belong to a holy God; you are not like the nations around you; you are set apart. The dinner table became a daily sermon on consecration. What could be more effective at keeping a truth before a people than to attach it to their food? Every bite said, "You are the LORD's, and you are different."

verseByVerse.quote: These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales... you may eat. But anything in the seas or the rivers that has not fins and scales... is detestable to you... And these you shall detest among the birds...
verseByVerse.commentary: The distinctions extend to the water and the air — fish with fins and scales are clean, the rest unclean; certain birds, mostly birds of prey and carrion-eaters, are off-limits; flying insects are largely forbidden, with a few exceptions like the locust. Scholars have long debated the exact rationale behind each category, and Scripture does not fully explain it. But the overarching purpose is clear and repeated: to make Israel a people who continually distinguish, who order even their appetites around belonging to God. There may be a further lesson in the details — the excluded predators and scavengers, creatures of violence and death, quietly reinforcing that God's people are to have nothing to do with death and corruption. But the heart of it is separateness. God was training a whole nation, meal by meal, to live as those set apart. And every one of these distinctions pointed forward to a day when the deeper reality would come and the shadow could pass — when clean and unclean would be redefined not by diet but by the cleansing blood of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24-47 — Uncleanness, Death, and 'Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns to the defilement that comes from touching dead bodies — carcasses of animals, creatures that die — and how such uncleanness must be dealt with. Then comes the great heartbeat of the whole book, the reason behind every law: "I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy." The endless distinctions all serve one end: a people made holy because their God is holy.
verseByVerse.theology: Contact with death defiles (vv.24-40) — a running theme in Leviticus, for death is the wage of sin (Rom 6:23) and the great intruder into God's good creation. The chapter's climax, "be holy, for I am holy" (vv.44-45), is the theme verse of Leviticus, quoted by Peter as the abiding call on the new-covenant people (1 Pet 1:16). The ground of holiness is not fear but relationship: "I am the LORD your God" who redeemed you (v.45). We are holy because we are his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a people surrounded by reminders of death were taught to keep separate from it, and to hear over all their laws the call: be holy, for I am holy.

Now: that call still stands, lifted straight into the New Testament: "as he who called you is holy, you also be holy" (1 Pet 1:15-16). Holiness is not a burden but the birthright of those who belong to a holy God.

verseByVerse.quote: And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening... Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten. You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing...
verseByVerse.commentary: Much of the rest of the chapter deals with defilement from contact with dead bodies — the carcasses of unclean animals, creatures that die on their own, the swarming things of the ground. Touch them, and you are unclean until evening; you must wash, and wait. Running underneath all of this is a theme that haunts the whole book of Leviticus: death defiles. Death is the great intruder, the wage of sin (Rom 6:23), the enemy that has no place in the presence of the living God. To be near death is to be reminded of the curse, and so it renders a person temporarily unfit to approach the Holy One. These laws pressed upon Israel, again and again, that they served a God of life, and that death and corruption cannot come casually into his presence. It is a shadow that aches for resolution — for the day when One would come who touches the dead and, instead of being defiled, raises them (Luke 7:14-15), and who would finally swallow up death itself in victory (1 Cor 15:54).

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy... For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: And now, out of all the detailed distinctions, rises the great refrain that is the heartbeat of Leviticus and the reason behind every law in it: "Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy." Here is why the clean and unclean, the holy and the common, matter so much. It is not about arbitrary rules; it is about reflecting the character of God. Israel is to be holy because God is holy — set apart because he is set apart, distinct because he is distinct. And notice the ground of the command: "I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God." Holiness is not the price of God's love but the response to it. He redeemed them first; now they are to live as his. This is the verse Peter lifts straight into the New Testament and lays on the church: "as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet 1:15-16). The food laws have passed; the call has not. We are still a people redeemed to reflect a holy God — not by what we eat, but by whole lives set apart to him.

11.theology:
Separation unto God. The dietary laws trained Israel, at every meal, in the distinction between holy and common — a people visibly set apart.

'Be holy, for I am holy.' The defining refrain (11:44-45), grounded in God's character and his redemptive act, quoted by Peter for the church (1 Pet 1:16).

Fulfilled in Christ. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and abolished the Jew-Gentile wall (Acts 10); the call to holiness endures, now defined by union with Christ.
11.examples:
Then: An Israelite, choosing what to eat, was reminded three times a day that he belonged to a holy God and a set-apart people, distinct from the nations around him.

Now: We are no longer bound by kosher laws, but the call to be holy and distinct is heightened in Christ. 'As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct' (1 Pet 1:15).

12.title: Purification After Childbirth: The Offering of the Poor
12.text: <sup>6</sup>And when the days of her purifying are completed... she shall bring to the priest... a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering... <sup>8</sup>And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons...
12.overview:
This brief chapter addresses purification after childbirth. To modern sensibilities it can seem strange, even offensive — why should the joyful, God-ordained act of bringing forth life render a woman ceremonially unclean? But we must read it within Leviticus's symbolic world. The issue is not that childbirth is sinful, but that it involves the flow of blood, and blood is life, and the loss of life-fluid touches the deep biblical association between fallenness, mortality, and the need for cleansing. Every birth, since Eden, comes trailing the shadow of the curse — "in pain you shall bring forth children" (Gen 3:16) — and every new life born is a life born into a world of sin and death, needing redemption.

Wenham notes that the purification ritual does not stigmatize motherhood; it dignifies it by drawing it into the sphere of God's holiness. The mother brings a burnt offering and a sin offering, and is pronounced clean. The wonder of birth is honored, and the reality of a fallen world is acknowledged, both at once.

But the chapter's deepest glory shines in the New Testament. For Luke records that Mary and Joseph fulfilled exactly this law for the infant Jesus: "And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses... they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord... and to offer a sacrifice... 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons'" (Luke 2:22–24). Two birds — the offering specifically appointed in 12:8 for those who could not afford a lamb. The offering of the poor.

Stop and feel the weight of it. The Lamb of God himself was brought to the temple, and for him was offered the poor woman's two birds — because the Holy Family could not afford a lamb. They did not need to buy a lamb; they were carrying him. The Maker of heaven and earth entered our world in such poverty that his mother brought the cheapest legal offering. "Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9). Leviticus 12, fulfilled in a Bethlehem-born baby, becomes one of the tenderest gospel windows in all the Old Testament.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the birth of a child, a mother enters a period of ceremonial uncleanness and then purification, after which she brings an offering — a lamb, or, if she cannot afford one, two birds. This is not a verdict that childbirth is sinful; it is holy and blessed. But the blood and discharge of birth touch the deep themes of life, blood, and our fallen condition — and quietly remind us that every child born is another soul who enters the world needing atonement.
verseByVerse.theology: The law is not a judgment on motherhood — children are a blessing (Ps 127:3) — but the loss of blood (the seat of life) and the entrance of another sinner into the world touch the truths of mortality and inherited sin (Ps 51:5). The required offerings include a sin offering, a sober acknowledgment that we are "brought forth in iniquity." The graded provision (a lamb, or two birds for the poor, v.8) is the very law Mary fulfilled, bringing "two turtledoves" (Luke 2:24) — revealing that the Savior was born into a poor family, and that he, the Law-giver, was born under the law to redeem those under it (Gal 4:4-5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a new mother brought her offering — a lamb if she could, two birds if she could not — and was pronounced clean, welcomed back to the worship of God.

Now: Mary brought the poor woman's offering for the birth of the Son of God (Luke 2:24). The King entered our world in poverty and under the law, to lift us out of both.

verseByVerse.quote: If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days... And when the days of her purifying are completed... she shall bring to the priest a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering... And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons... And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary: This short chapter can trouble a modern reader: why should the joyful, God-blessed act of bearing a child leave a mother ceremonially unclean? We must be careful. The law is not calling motherhood sinful — children are "a heritage from the LORD" (Ps 127:3), and the command to be fruitful is a blessing. The uncleanness has to do with the blood and discharge of childbirth, and blood in Leviticus always touches the deep and sacred realities of life and death. There may also be a quieter, more searching truth here: every child brought into the world, however precious, is another sinner entering a fallen race, one who will need atonement — for we are all "brought forth in iniquity" (Ps 51:5). That is why the purification includes a sin offering. But the tenderest thing in the chapter is the provision for the poor: if she cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do. And this is the very law that Mary kept. When she and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple, they offered "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" (Luke 2:24) — the offering of the poor. The King of glory was born into a family too poor to bring a lamb; the Lawgiver himself was "born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law" (Gal 4:4-5). He entered our poverty and submitted to our law, to make us rich and set us free.

12.theology:
Born into a fallen world. Even the joy of birth, marked by blood, points to the universal need for cleansing — every life enters the shadow of sin and death.

Atonement scaled to poverty. The provision of two birds for the poor (12:8) shows that no one is shut out from God by want.

The poverty of Christ. Mary's offering of two birds (Luke 2:24) reveals that the Lamb of God entered the world in real poverty — 'for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9).
12.examples:
Then: A new mother in Israel, after the appointed days, brought her offering — a lamb if she could, two birds if she could not — and was pronounced clean before the LORD.

Now: We marvel that Mary brought the offering of the poor for the Son of God. The King of glory met us in poverty; let no one think themselves too lowly for his grace.

13.title: Skin Disease: The Priest Who Examines
13.text: <sup>2</sup>When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest... <sup>45</sup>The leprous person... shall cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.' <sup>46</sup>...He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the long, painstaking law of tsara'at — usually translated "leprosy," though it covers a range of skin conditions and even mold in fabrics. The priest is appointed as the examiner, the one who looks closely, declares clean or unclean, and pronounces the verdict. The detail is exhausting precisely because the stakes are so high: a wrong diagnosis means either a clean person banished or an unclean person spreading defilement through the camp.

The disease becomes, in Scripture's symbolic vocabulary, the great picture of sin: it spreads, it disfigures, it works beneath the surface and erupts visibly, it isolates, and it makes one unfit for the presence of God. The verdict "unclean" carries a terrible weight — the leper must tear his clothes, cover his lip, cry "Unclean, unclean," and live alone outside the camp (13:45–46). Cut off from worship, from family, from community — a living picture of the alienation that sin works.

Sproul and Ferguson both draw the line: this is what sin does to the soul. It defiles, it spreads, it cuts off from God and others, and no amount of self-cleansing can reverse it. The leper could not heal himself; he could only be examined and declared. The priest's verdict was final and the sentence was exile.

And here the heart aches for the Great Priest who is coming. For the law could only diagnose; it could not cure. The priest could declare a leper unclean but could not make him clean. Then came One who, when a leper fell before him crying "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean," stretched out his hand and touched him — the unthinkable, defiling touch — and said, "I will; be clean" (Matt 8:2–3). He did not become unclean by the touch; the leper became clean. The Great High Priest both examines and heals, both pronounces the verdict and bears it away. Where Aaron could only send the leper outside the camp, Jesus "suffered outside the gate" (Heb 13:12) to bring the outcast home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Leprous Disease and the Priest's Examination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A long, careful chapter on "leprous disease" (Hebrew tsara'at, a range of skin afflictions, not only modern leprosy). The priest becomes examiner, inspecting the swelling, the spot, the raw flesh, the white hair, quarantining the person for seven days, looking again, watching whether the disease spreads. It reads like a medical manual, but its deeper subject is impurity — a disease that spreads, defiles, and isolates. In it Israel had a living, visible picture of what sin does to the soul.
verseByVerse.theology: Leprosy in Scripture is the great emblem of sin: it starts small, spreads relentlessly, renders unclean, cuts a person off from the community and the sanctuary, and lies beyond self-cure. The priest cannot heal it, only diagnose it — the law can expose our defilement but cannot cleanse it (Rom 3:20). The leper's fate — excluded, dwelling alone, outside the camp (vv.45-46) — pictures the alienation sin brings. And it sets the stage for the wonder of the Gospels, where Jesus does what no priest could: he reaches out and touches the leper, and instead of being defiled, he makes the leper clean (Mark 1:41).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the afflicted Israelite stood before the priest in dread, watched for signs of spreading disease, and, if unclean, was sent to live alone outside the camp.

Now: sin is the deeper leprosy — it spreads, defiles, isolates, and we cannot cure ourselves. But One has come who touches the untouchable and makes the unclean clean (Mark 1:41). The leper's cry becomes our confession, and his cleansing our hope.

verseByVerse.quote: When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest... The priest shall examine the diseased area... and shut up the diseased person for seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens by making the priest an examiner. When a suspicious mark appears on the skin — a swelling, an eruption, a bright spot — the person is brought to the priest, who inspects it closely: Is the hair in it turned white? Does it appear deeper than the skin? If the case is unclear, he shuts the person up for seven days and looks again, watching one thing above all — whether it is spreading. Notice what the priest can and cannot do. He can examine, diagnose, declare clean or unclean; but he cannot heal. The whole apparatus is about detection, not cure. And here is the first great lesson, for leprosy is Scripture's living picture of sin. Like this disease, sin often starts as a small spot, easily ignored; and like it, sin spreads, working its way deeper and wider until it defiles the whole. The law, like the priest here, is expert at exposing our condition — "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Rom 3:20) — but it cannot cleanse us. It can only pronounce the verdict: unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man is afflicted with a leprous disease, he shall be brought to the priest... if the leprous disease has covered all his body, he shall pronounce him clean of the disease; it has all turned white, and he is clean. But when raw flesh appears on him, he shall be unclean... The priest shall examine it, and if the disease has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary: The examinations grow more detailed — chronic disease, raw flesh, an old boil, a burn that has healed and then broken out again. In each case the priest looks for the same telltale signs: white hair, spreading, depth, raw flesh. There is a striking detail in verse 13: if the disease has covered the man's whole body and turned it all white, he is pronounced clean; but the moment raw flesh appears, he is unclean. Whatever the medical explanation, there is a spiritual echo worth hearing. The person who is thoroughly covered — who has come to the end of himself and admitted the fullness of his condition — can be dealt with; it is the festering, hidden, half-acknowledged wound, the raw flesh still active, that defiles. So it is with sin: the one who confesses the whole of his sinfulness finds mercy, while the one who nurses a secret, active corruption remains unclean. The priest's patient, repeated examination reminds us that sin must be taken seriously, watched, not shrugged off — for its nature is to spread.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man or woman has a disease on the head or the beard... an itching disease... And if the disease breaks out in the skin... the priest shall pronounce him unclean; his disease is on his head. The leprous person who has the disease... he is unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary: Still more cases follow — diseases of the head and beard, the itch, the difference between true leprous disease and a harmless rash or ordinary baldness. The sheer length and care of these chapters make their own point: God takes defilement seriously, down to the smallest spot, and will not let his people grow careless about what makes them unclean. Every possible case is considered, every ambiguity examined, because holiness matters that much. We may find the detail tedious, but it is mercy in disguise — God refusing to let a single defiling thing slip by unnoticed among a people he means to dwell with. And it presses home the hopelessness of the human condition apart from grace: case after case, the verdict falls, "unclean," and the priest has no remedy to offer, only a diagnosis. The law can name the disease of sin with perfect accuracy. It cannot cure it. For that, we must wait for a Physician the law could not provide.

verseByVerse.quote: The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.' He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary: The leper outside the camp is one of the most powerful and heartbreaking images in the entire Old Testament. Torn garments, loose hair, a covered lip, and the mournful cry going before him: "Unclean, unclean." Alone. Outside the community, barred from the sanctuary, cut off from the fellowship of God's people and the presence of God. This is what sin does: it isolates, it excludes, it drives a person outside the camp, away from God and from others. The leper who cries "Unclean!" is forced into an awful, public honesty about his own condition — and honesty about our uncleanness is the very thing the gospel requires of us, though the church calls it confession. Now hold this picture beside the Gospels, and feel the wonder. When a leper came to Jesus, the law said the clean must keep away from the unclean, lest the defilement spread. But Jesus "stretched out his hand and touched him" (Mark 1:41) — and the flow ran backward. The leper's uncleanness did not defile Jesus; Jesus' holiness cleansed the leper. And on the cross, our Lord went outside the camp himself (Heb 13:12), taking the leper's place, bearing our uncleanness, crying our cry, so that we — unclean, isolated, shut out — might be brought in, made clean, and welcomed home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with "leprous disease" in fabric — a spreading greenish or reddish contamination in wool, linen, or leather. The same procedure applies: the priest examines it, shuts it up seven days, watches whether it spreads. If it persists, the garment is burned. Defilement can cling even to things, and what cannot be cleansed must be destroyed. Sin's corruption reaches further than we think.
verseByVerse.theology: That contamination could infect garments and had to be burned if it would not wash out (vv.52-57) extends the lesson: sin's defilement clings and spreads beyond the person into the things around him, and what cannot be cleansed must be destroyed. It anticipates the seriousness with which sin must finally be dealt — purged by fire or washed clean (cf. Jude 23, "hating even the garment stained by the flesh"). Only what God cleanses can be kept.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even a stained garment was examined, quarantined, and if the corruption persisted, burned — defilement was never treated lightly.

Now: sin corrupts more than we imagine, spreading into our habits, homes, and belongings. We are to deal with it ruthlessly, "hating even the garment stained by the flesh" (Jude 23), keeping only what Christ has cleansed.

verseByVerse.quote: When there is a case of leprous disease in a garment, whether a woolen or a linen garment... the priest shall examine the disease and shut up that which has the disease for seven days... And he shall burn the garment... It is a persistent leprous disease; it shall be burned in the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: Surprisingly, the chapter closes not with people but with clothing — a spreading, corrupting mark in wool, linen, or leather (perhaps mold or mildew). The same careful process is followed: the priest examines it, shuts it up for seven days, and watches whether it spreads. If washing removes it, well and good; but if the corruption persists, the garment must be burned in the fire. Why include even this? Because it teaches that defilement is not confined to the body; it clings to things, spreads into the objects of daily life, and reaches further than we would like to think. And what cannot be cleansed must be destroyed. There is a sober lesson here about the reach and the seriousness of sin. Its corruption is not neatly contained; it works its way into our habits, our homes, our belongings, our relationships. And it must be dealt with ruthlessly. Jude uses this very imagery, urging us to show mercy to sinners while "hating even the garment stained by the flesh" (Jude 23). Whatever God's fire cannot be trusted to purify must be given up. Only what he cleanses may be kept.

13.theology:
Sin's nature pictured. Skin disease, working beneath the surface and erupting visibly, images sin: it defiles, spreads, disfigures, and cuts off from God.

The priest's verdict. The priest could diagnose and declare but not cure; only the Great High Priest both pronounces and heals.

Outside the camp. The exile of the leper is reversed by Christ, who 'suffered outside the gate' (Heb 13:12) to bring the outcast home.
13.examples:
Then: A suspected leper was brought to the priest, examined, and, if diseased, sent out of the camp to live alone, crying 'Unclean' — cut off from worship and community.

Now: We bring our defilement honestly to the Great Priest, who does not banish us but touches us and makes us clean, having taken our place outside the camp.

14.title: The Cleansing of the Leper: Two Birds and Living Water
14.text: <sup>4</sup>the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds and cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop. <sup>6</sup>...he shall dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water. <sup>7</sup>...and shall let the living bird go into the open field.
14.overview:
If chapter 13 is the law of diagnosis, chapter 14 is the liturgy of restoration — and it is breathtaking. For here, against all expectation, the law makes provision for what it could not produce: the cleansing of a healed leper, his joyful return to the camp and the worship of God. The ritual is among the most vividly gospel-shaped in all of Leviticus.

The centerpiece is the rite of the two birds (14:4–7). Two clean birds are taken. One is killed over fresh (literally "living") water in an earthen vessel, its blood mingling with the running water. The living bird, together with cedarwood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, is dipped in the blood of the slain bird. Then the priest sprinkles the cleansed leper seven times — and releases the living bird into the open field, to fly away free.

Wenham and many after him have seen the unmistakable shape of the gospel here. One bird dies; the other, dipped in the blood of the first, is set free to soar into the open sky. Is this not death and resurrection? The slain bird is Christ crucified, his blood mingled with living water (recall the blood and water from his side, John 19:34); the released bird is Christ risen, ascending free into the heavens, and with him the cleansed sinner soars into liberty. The hyssop recalls the Passover and reappears at the cross (John 19:29); the scarlet, the blood; the cedar, the enduring tree.

The leper, once exiled and crying "Unclean," is now sprinkled, washed, shaved, and brought back — back to the camp, back to his family, back to the worship of God. This is the homecoming of the outcast, the resurrection of the living dead. And every cleansed leper is a portrait of every sinner saved by grace: brought from the place of death, washed in blood, sealed by the Spirit, and welcomed home — while the living bird, dipped in saving blood, flies free into the open field of the new creation. "If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed" (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-32 — The Cleansing of the Leper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If chapter 13 left the leper outside the camp with no cure, chapter 14 brings astonishing good news: there is a ritual for "the day of his cleansing." When God has healed a leper, the priest goes out to him — outside the camp — and performs a beautiful ceremony with two birds: one is killed, and the other is dipped in its blood and set free to fly away. Then, over eight days, the cleansed man is washed, shaved, and brought back with offerings, blood placed on his ear, thumb, and toe like a priest being consecrated. The outcast is restored to God and to his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The two birds are a vivid gospel picture: one dies, the other, dipped in the death-blood, is released alive into the open field — death and resurrection, judgment borne and freedom given (cf. Rom 4:25). The priest goes "outside the camp" to the leper (v.3), as Christ came to us in our uncleanness. The cedar, scarlet yarn, and hyssop are the tools of purification (cf. Ps 51:7, "purge me with hyssop"). And the blood on ear, thumb, and toe (v.14) — the very rite of priestly ordination (8:23-24) — means the cleansed leper is not merely readmitted but consecrated, restored to full fellowship. This is the ritual Jesus honored: "show yourself to the priest" (Matt 8:4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the healed leper watched one bird die and another fly free in its blood, and was washed, restored, and welcomed home — an outcast made clean and brought near.

Now: Christ, our slain and risen substitute, has cleansed us who were unclean and brought us from "outside the camp" into the family of God. The bird set free is every sinner released by the blood of the Lamb (Rom 4:25).

verseByVerse.quote: This shall be the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp... he shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds... And he shall kill one of the birds... He shall take the live bird... and dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed... and he shall let the living bird go into the open field.
verseByVerse.commentary: After the hopelessness of chapter 13, this chapter breaks like sunrise: "the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing." There is a day of cleansing. The outcast can come home. And notice the first, tender detail: the priest "shall go out of the camp" to him. The leper cannot come in; so the priest goes out to where the unclean man is — a shadow of the Savior who came out to us in our defilement. Then the ceremony of the two birds, and it is pure gospel. Two clean birds are taken. One is killed, its blood caught in a bowl of fresh water. The other is dipped alive into the blood of the first, and then — released, set free to fly away into the open sky. Do you see it? One bird dies; the other, marked with the death-blood, goes free. It is death and resurrection in feathers and blood: the substitute slain, and the cleansed one released alive, soaring away because another died in its place. "He was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification" (Rom 4:25). The cedar and scarlet and hyssop are the instruments of cleansing (Ps 51:7); the washing and shaving mark a new beginning. The unclean man is clean, and the freed bird is his own soul, released by blood.

verseByVerse.quote: On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish... The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot... And if he is poor and cannot afford so much... he shall take one male lamb...
verseByVerse.commentary: The cleansing is not complete until the man is fully restored, and the eighth-day ritual does exactly that. He brings guilt, sin, and burnt offerings, and then — remarkably — the priest puts blood on the lobe of his right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot. Where have we seen that before? It is the rite of priestly ordination (8:23-24). The cleansed leper is treated like a priest being consecrated. He is not merely allowed back through the gate on sufferance; he is restored to full, honored fellowship, his whole life — what he hears, what he does, where he walks — claimed again for God. This is how completely God restores the sinner he cleanses: not as a second-class citizen, but as one consecrated to himself. And once more, the tenderness for the poor: if the man cannot afford two lambs, one lamb and two birds will do (v.21). No one is too poor to be fully restored. When God cleanses, he cleanses all the way, and he does it for prince and pauper alike. This was the very law Jesus told the leper he healed to fulfill — "go, show yourself to the priest" (Matt 8:4) — sending the cleansed man to enact this beautiful ritual of restoration.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally, the strange case of "leprous disease" in a house — a spreading greenish or reddish growth in the walls (perhaps mold). The priest examines it, orders the affected stones removed and the house scraped; if it returns, the whole house is torn down. But there is grace even here: a house can be cleansed with the same two-bird ritual and declared clean. Corruption reaches even into our dwellings — and God provides for cleansing there too.
verseByVerse.theology: That defilement could infect a house, requiring removal of stones or demolition (vv.40-45), yet also could be cleansed by the two-bird rite (vv.48-53), shows both the reach of corruption and the reach of grace. Sin spreads into the very structures of our lives; but God's cleansing reaches as far as sin does. Nothing is beyond either the contamination of sin or the power of atoning blood to make clean.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: even a contaminated house could be cleansed by blood and declared clean, or torn down if the corruption would not leave — God's grace reaching into the walls.

Now: sin corrupts our homes and structures, but the cleansing power of Christ's blood reaches everywhere sin does. No corner of life is beyond his power to make clean.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house... the priest shall go in to examine the house... they shall take out the stones in which is the disease and throw them into an unclean place... And he shall take to cleanse the house two birds... So he shall make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary: The strangest case of all closes the chapter: "leprous disease" in a house — a spreading, discolored growth in the plaster and stones, likely a destructive mold. The priest inspects it, orders the infected stones pulled out and thrown away and the walls scraped clean; if it comes back, the whole house must be demolished, stone by stone. But then, grace: a house that can be cleansed is purified with the same two-bird ritual as the leper, and "it shall be clean." Two truths stand side by side here. First, the reach of corruption. Sin's defilement does not stay tidily contained in the individual; it seeps into the structures around us — our homes, our institutions, the walls we live within. It spreads. It must be dealt with, sometimes by removing what is infected, sometimes by tearing the whole thing down. But second, and sweeter, the reach of grace. God's cleansing extends as far as sin's contamination — even to a house, even to the walls, even with the same atoning blood. Wherever sin has crept, the blood of the Lamb can reach and make clean. There is no corner of our lives so infected that it lies beyond the power of Christ to cleanse.

14.theology:
Death and resurrection. The two birds — one slain, one freed in its blood — portray the gospel: Christ crucified and risen, and the sinner set free to soar.

Blood and water. The slain bird over living water anticipates the blood and water from Christ's pierced side (John 19:34) — atonement and cleansing together.

From outcast to priest. The cleansed leper is consecrated like a priest; grace does not merely readmit but elevates the forgiven to holy service.
14.examples:
Then: A healed leper watched one bird die and another fly free in its blood, was sprinkled seven times, washed, and brought home — restored to family, community, and worship.

Now: Every sinner cleansed by Christ is the leper brought home: washed in blood, raised to new life, set free to soar, and consecrated as a priest to God.

15.title: Bodily Discharges: The Pervasiveness of Defilement
15.text: <sup>31</sup>Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 completes the section on clean and unclean by addressing bodily discharges — the most intimate and unavoidable realities of human physical life. Normal and abnormal flows alike render one ceremonially unclean. The effect of the chapter, when read whole, is to teach the sheer pervasiveness of ritual uncleanness. It touches everyone, repeatedly, in the ordinary course of bodily existence. No one can escape it; everyone needs cleansing again and again.

This is precisely the point. Wenham argues that the very inescapability of uncleanness is the lesson: it teaches the inescapability of sin's contamination. Just as no Israelite could pass through life without becoming ceremonially unclean, so no human being can pass through life without becoming morally defiled. The contamination is woven into our very nature; it touches everything we are and do. The chapter is a sustained sermon on total depravity — not that we are as bad as we could be, but that no part of us is untouched by the fall.

And the climax (15:31) reveals the deadly seriousness: this is all about being able to dwell near "my tabernacle that is in their midst." Uncleanness defiles the sanctuary; it threatens the very thing Israel most needs — the presence of God among them. The whole elaborate system exists to guard that presence.

Then comes the gospel reversal that takes the breath away. In Mark 5, a woman with a flow of blood for twelve years — a woman who, by this very chapter, was perpetually unclean, perpetually contagious, cut off from worship and ordinary human touch for over a decade — pushes through the crowd to touch the hem of Jesus' garment. By every rule of Leviticus 15, her touch should have made him unclean. Instead, "immediately the flow of blood dried up" (Mark 5:29), and Jesus, far from recoiling, says, "Daughter... your faith has made you well; go in peace" (Mark 5:34). The current of contamination is reversed. Where uncleanness once flowed from the defiled to the holy, now cleansing flows from the Holy One to the defiled. Jesus does not catch our uncleanness; he heals it. The pervasive defilement of Leviticus 15 meets its match in the more pervasive grace of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This chapter deals with ceremonial uncleanness from bodily discharges — both male and female, both from disease and from the natural functions of the body. Anyone with such a discharge, and much they touch, becomes unclean until washed and until evening. The point is stated plainly at the end: God dwells among his people, so they must be kept from defiling his sanctuary. Even the most private and ordinary realities of the body are brought under the truth that a holy God lives in their midst.
verseByVerse.theology: These laws again connect bodily emissions — which touch the springs of life and its loss — to ceremonial uncleanness, teaching that fallen life is marked everywhere by impermanence and impurity. The stated purpose is protective: "keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst" (v.31). Because God dwells with them, holiness touches everything. And the gospel note is stunning: the woman with a twelve-year discharge (Mark 5:25-34), permanently unclean under this law, touched Jesus — and instead of defiling him, she was healed, and he called her "daughter." In Christ, the flow of contagion reverses forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman unclean for years by a discharge of blood lived cut off from normal worship and touch — until she reached out to Jesus (Mark 5:27).

Now: what would have made Jesus unclean instead made the woman whole. He is not defiled by our uncleanness; he cleanses it. Reach out and touch him, and hear him say, "Daughter... be healed" (Mark 5:34).

verseByVerse.quote: When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean... Everything on which the one with the discharge lies shall be unclean... And when the one with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes... and he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter turns to a delicate subject: ceremonial uncleanness arising from bodily discharges, here concerning men — some from disease, some from the ordinary functions of the body. The one with a discharge is unclean, and so are the things he lies or sits on, and those who touch them. Washing and the passing of time restore cleanness. We may find these laws strange, even uncomfortable, but they carry a consistent message. In a fallen world, the very springs of life are touched by impermanence and impurity; the body, wonderful as it is, is also a place of decay and loss. Nothing about human existence, not even its most private and ordinary aspects, lies outside the reach of the truth that we are a fallen people needing cleansing. God is not embarrassed to legislate about the body, because he made it and means to sanctify the whole of life. And every washing, every "until the evening," quietly points to a deeper cleansing that no amount of water can accomplish — one that would come only through blood.

verseByVerse.quote: When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days... If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days... all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness... And the priest shall make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same principles apply to women, including the natural monthly cycle and, more seriously, a prolonged discharge of blood. A woman with such a chronic condition would be continually unclean, cut off from normal worship and from the ordinary touch of family and community — a lonely, wearing exile. And it is precisely here that one of the most beautiful moments in the Gospels comes into focus. Remember the woman who "had had a discharge of blood for twelve years" (Mark 5:25). Under this very law she was permanently unclean, and by these rules her touch would defile whomever she touched. That is why she came trembling, secretly, from behind, and only dared to touch the fringe of Jesus' garment. And what happened? The contagion ran backward. Instead of her uncleanness defiling him, his cleanness healed her; the flow of blood that had exiled her for twelve years stopped at his touch. And far from recoiling, he turned and called her "Daughter" (Mark 5:34). Here is the gospel that all of Leviticus is straining toward: in Jesus, holiness is stronger than defilement. He does not keep the unclean at arm's length; he touches them, and makes them clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now, at last, the reason behind all these laws of cleanness is stated outright: "that they may not die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst." There it is. The whole elaborate system of clean and unclean exists because of one staggering fact — God dwells among his people. His holy tabernacle stands in the very center of the camp, and holiness cannot coexist casually with defilement. Because God is near, everything matters; because the Holy One lives in their midst, even the body's ordinary functions come under the call to holiness. This is not the fussiness of a distant deity; it is the seriousness of an intimate one. The nearer God draws, the more his holiness touches every corner of life. And this is our situation too, more than Israel's: for the Spirit of God now dwells not in a tent among us but in us — "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1 Cor 6:19). The God who guarded his dwelling so carefully has made our very bodies his home. Holiness, then, is not less urgent for us but more — because he is nearer than ever.

15.theology:
The pervasiveness of defilement. The inescapability of ritual uncleanness teaches the inescapability of sin's contamination — no part of us is untouched by the fall.

Guarding God's presence. The purity laws exist to protect the dwelling of God among his people (15:31), the very thing Israel could not live without.

The reversal in Christ. The woman of Mark 5, perpetually unclean, touches Jesus and is healed — in Christ, holiness is the stronger contagion, and cleansing flows from him to us.
15.examples:
Then: Every Israelite, through ordinary bodily life, repeatedly became unclean and needed cleansing — a daily lesson in the all-pervading reach of defilement.

Now: Like the bleeding woman, we come unclean to Jesus, and his touch does not defile him but heals us. The flow of grace reverses the flow of contamination.

16.title: The Day of Atonement: The Heart of the Gospel
16.text: <sup>2</sup>..."Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat... so that he may not die." <sup>15</sup>Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering... and bring its blood inside the veil... and sprinkle it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. <sup>21</sup>And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel... <sup>22</sup>The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area...
16.overview:
We come now to the summit. If Leviticus is a mountain range, chapter 16 is its Everest; if the whole Old Testament sacrificial system is a great cathedral, the Day of Atonement is its high altar. Here, once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest did what was done on no other day: he passed through the veil into the Most Holy Place, into the immediate presence of God, bearing blood. Everything in the book has been building to this. Carson rightly calls Hebrews 9–10 the inspired commentary on this chapter, and we will not be able to read it without weeping.

First, the awful approach. Aaron may not come "at any time" into the Holy Place "so that he may not die" (16:2). Only on this one day, and only by blood. He sets aside his glorious garments and dresses in simple linen — the high priest humbled, stripped of splendor, to enter as a servant. He offers a bull for his own sin first, for even the high priest is a sinner. Then he takes the blood and the incense, and passes alone through the veil, into the blinding presence of the Holy One, where the cloud of glory dwells above the mercy seat.

Then, the two goats — the theological heart of the chapter and perhaps of the entire Bible. Lots are cast. One goat is for the LORD; it is slaughtered, and its blood is carried within the veil and sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, the atonement cover over the ark. This is propitiation — the turning away of wrath, the satisfaction of justice, the blood presented before the throne of God himself. The second goat is for Azazel; over its head Aaron lays both hands and confesses all the sins of Israel, transferring them to the animal, which is then led away into the wilderness, never to return. This is expiation — the bearing away of sin, its removal "as far as the east is from the west" (Ps 103:12). Two goats, one truth: sin must be both paid for (the blood on the mercy seat) and carried away (the scapegoat into the wilderness). Keller loved to say that on the cross both happened at once — Jesus is both the goat slain and the goat sent away, both our propitiation and our expiation.

And oh, the glory of the fulfillment. The mercy seat — the hilasterion, the place of atonement — is the very word Paul uses of Christ: "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25). Christ is the mercy seat, the place where blood meets the broken law and wrath is satisfied. He entered "once for all into the holy places... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). Aaron entered yearly, with another's blood, trembling lest he die; Christ entered once, with his own blood, and sat down. And when he died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt 27:51) — the veil that barred the way ripped open by the hand of God, the road into the Most Holy Place flung wide forever.
