Sproul never tired of saying that the mercy seat is where the holiness of God and the mercy of God kiss. There, the blood covers the broken law beneath; there, justice and love embrace. And from the cross came the cry that ended all the sacrifices forever: "It is finished" (John 19:30). The scapegoat has carried our sin beyond the reach of memory; the blood is on the mercy seat; the veil is torn; the way is open. Holy, holy, holy — and we may come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 - Before the Veil: How Aaron May Enter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most solemn day of Israel's year opens not with ceremony but with a grave: "after the death of the two sons of Aaron" (v.1). Nadab and Abihu had rushed into God's presence with strange fire, and died. So the whole chapter is God's answer to a burning question — how may a sinful man come near a holy God and live? The answer is: not at any time, not any way he pleases, but only on this one day, only by blood, and only as God prescribes. Aaron lays aside his golden splendor and dresses in plain linen, bathes, and gathers a bull for his own sin and two goats for the people's. Before he touches anyone else's guilt, he must reckon with his own. Then the lots are cast over the two goats — one for the LORD, one for Azazel — the two halves of a single mercy about to unfold.
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is God's gift, not man's right. The death of Nadab and Abihu stands at the door of this chapter as a warning written in blood: God will be treated as holy (Lev 10:3). Yet the same God who says "not at any time" opens "this way" (v.3) — grace hedged by holiness. And that the high priest must atone for himself first (v.6) exposes the flaw in every earthly mediator: he is himself a sinner. It makes us ache for a priest who needs no sacrifice for his own sin (Heb 7:26-27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: no Israelite could stroll into God's presence; even the high priest entered trembling, once a year, by blood, or died.

Now: we have a High Priest "holy, innocent, unstained" who offered no sacrifice for Himself because He had no sin — and who bids us "draw near with confidence" (Heb 4:16). The linen Aaron put on, Christ was: perfect righteousness. We come clothed not in our splendor but in His.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron... Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat... so that he may not die.
verseByVerse.commentary: The date-stamp is a grave. Nadab and Abihu had offered "unauthorized fire before the LORD" and were consumed (Lev 10:1-2); now their father is told plainly why the veil exists. It is not decoration but a barrier — a "keep out" sewn in blue and purple and scarlet, guarding the mercy seat where God said "I will appear in the cloud." The lesson lands hard on us who speak so casually of coming to God: the Holy One cannot be approached "at any time," on a whim, in a manner of our own choosing. The wonder of the gospel is not that God lowered the barrier but that He Himself passed through it — and then, at the cross, tore it from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). Feel both the terror and the tenderness here: the God who says "lest he die" is the God who would die that we might live.

verseByVerse.quote: But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering... He shall put on the holy linen coat... He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on.
verseByVerse.commentary: "But in this way" — three words of pure grace. God does not only bar the door; He shows the way through it. Notice the change of clothes. On other days the high priest blazed with gold, blue, and precious stones, bells ringing as he moved (Ex 28). Today he strips it all off and puts on plain white linen, bathed and lowly, dressed like the humblest servant. The greater the day, the lower he stoops — a picture of our Lord, who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7), laying aside His glory to do the work of atonement. The goats and the ram come "from the congregation": the people supply the victims, for it is their sin being dealt with. Everything is provided; nothing is left to improvisation. Salvation is meticulous because holiness is not careless.

verseByVerse.quote: Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house... And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Aaron can carry anyone else's sin, he must deal with his own. The mediator kneels as a sinner first — a quiet confession that no son of Aaron is clean enough to save. This is the crack in the old priesthood that makes us long for a better one: a priest who has "no need... to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins" (Heb 7:27). Then the two goats are set before the LORD and lots are cast. The meaning of Azazel is debated — perhaps a name for the place of removal, or simply "the goat that goes away," the scapegoat. But the picture is unmistakable: two goats, one atonement. One will be killed and its blood carried in; the other sent away alive, carrying sin out. Sin must be both paid for and carried away — and at Calvary both goats meet in one Lord: Jesus is the goat slain and the goat sent away at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-19 - Within the Veil: Blood on the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the high priest does what no one else in Israel may do, and what he himself may do only today: he passes through the veil into the Most Holy Place, into the immediate presence of God. He carries a censer of burning coals and sweet incense, so that a cloud will veil the mercy seat "that he may not die" (v.13) — even the mediator must be shielded from the unclouded glory. Then comes the blood: first the bull's, for himself; then the goat's, for the people; sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, seven times over. The very sanctuary is cleansed "because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel" (v.16). This is the beating heart of Leviticus, and Hebrews 9—10 is its inspired commentary.
verseByVerse.theology: This is propitiation — blood presented before the throne of God to turn away wrath and satisfy justice. The mercy seat (Hebrew kapporet, the "atonement cover") is where the blood meets the broken law kept in the ark beneath it. Here holiness and mercy meet without either being compromised: the law is honored, the sinner is spared. Paul reaches for this very object when he says God put Christ forward as a "propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25) — Jesus is the true mercy seat. And note: even the sanctuary needs cleansing, because sin defiles everything it touches, and "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb 9:22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: once a year one man, alone, in a cloud of incense, sprinkled blood in the dark on a golden lid, and Israel's sins were covered for another year.

Now: Christ "entered once for all into the holy places... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). He needed no incense-cloud to survive God's presence — He is that presence. He did not sprinkle and withdraw; He sat down (Heb 10:12). What Aaron repeated every year because it was never finished, Christ did once because it was.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar... and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil... that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat... And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger... seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary: Watch the high priest disappear behind the curtain. He carries fire and incense, and a cloud rises to shroud the mercy seat — for no man, not even Aaron, can gaze on the unveiled glory and live. The incense is a mercy: it hides him. Then he sprinkles the blood of his own bull "on the front of the mercy seat... seven times" — seven, the number of completeness, atonement fully made. Picture it: the ark below holds the tablets of the law Israel has broken; the blood falls above them, between the broken law and the God who gave it. That golden lid is the most important object in the world that day, because it is where wrath and mercy meet. Here is the gospel in shadow — the law accuses from beneath, the blood answers from above, and God looks down not on our sin but on the sprinkled blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil... sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel...
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the people's goat. Its blood is carried where no Israelite could go, sprinkled where only God could see, "because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and... all their sins" (v.16). Notice what is being cleansed: not only the people but the place. Sin is so contaminating that it defiles even the tent where God consents to dwell "in the midst of their uncleannesses." Holiness and sin cannot share a room; either the sin is purged or the presence departs. So the blood goes everywhere — the Most Holy Place, the tent, the altar — each sprinkled seven times, each made clean. And while Aaron works, "no one may be in the tent of meeting" (v.17): atonement is a lonely labor. On the great Day of ours, too, the Mediator was utterly alone — "I have trodden the winepress alone" (Isa 63:3) — forsaken even by God, that we might never be.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-28 - Outside the Camp: Sin Carried Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blood has been presented; now sin must be removed. Aaron lays both hands on the head of the living goat and confesses over it "all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins" (v.21) — every category, nothing held back, pressed down onto the animal's head. Then the goat is led away by an appointed man into the wilderness, "to a remote area," and released where it can never find its way home. Israel watched it shrink to a dot on the horizon and vanish — and knew their sin was gone. Then the priest washes and reclothes, and the sin offerings are carried "outside the camp" and burned. Two movements, one atonement: sin paid for by blood, sin borne away by the goat.
verseByVerse.theology: This is expiation — the actual removal of guilt. The laying on of hands is a transfer: the sin of the people is reckoned to the substitute, and the substitute carries it away "to a remote area," never to return. It is Isaiah's gospel centuries early: "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6). And that the sin offerings are burned "outside the camp" is not lost on the New Testament: "So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood" (Heb 13:12). Our sin was carried out of the city, out of the camp, out of God's sight — as far as the east is from the west (Ps 103:12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a nation stood in silence and watched a goat carry their sins over the horizon until it disappeared, and they believed it was gone.

Now: we look not at a vanishing goat but at an empty tomb. Christ carried our sins not into a wilderness we might one day stumble back into, but into death itself, and left them there. When guilt whispers that the old sins are still on file, faith answers with the horizon: it is gone, borne away, out of reach forever. "There is therefore now no condemnation" (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins... The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is one of the most vivid pictures of salvation in all of Scripture. Aaron presses both hands on the goat's head — not a light touch but a leaning weight — and speaks aloud every kind of sin: iniquities (the crookedness of the heart), transgressions (deliberate rebellions), and sins (the failures and misses). Three words to leave nothing out; a whole year of a whole nation's guilt named over one head. Then the goat is led away and let go "in the wilderness," to a land cut off, never to return. Israel did not merely hear that their sin was forgiven; they watched it walk away. This is what your Savior did with your sin: He took it on His own head — "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6) — and carried it beyond recovery. It is not filed away. It is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments... and shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: With the sin borne away, the mood changes. Aaron washes, lays aside the plain linen, and puts his glorious garments back on — the servant's work done, the splendor restored. It is a small resurrection picture: humiliation, then glory; the linen of suffering exchanged for the robes of honor, as our Lord, having finished the work, was "crowned with glory and honor" (Heb 2:9). Now come the burnt offerings — whole animals given up entirely to God in the flames. Once sin has been dealt with, worship can rise. The order is everything and never changes: first atonement, then adoration; first the sin removed, then the life poured out in thankful surrender. We do not worship our way into acceptance; we are accepted, and so we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water... And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering... shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the man who handled the scapegoat, even the one who burns the carcasses, must wash before returning to the camp — sin's contamination clings to everything near it. And the bodies of the sin offerings are not eaten but carried "outside the camp" and burned to ash. The writer of Hebrews sees his Lord in that lonely fire beyond the gate: "So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured" (Heb 13:12-13). Golgotha was outside the city wall — the sin-bearer cast out as unclean, treated as sin itself, so that the unclean might be brought in. The place of shame became the place of cleansing. And the call to us is to go out to Him there, willing to share His reproach, because the camp of this world has nothing that compares.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-34 - A Statute Forever: The Sabbath of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally God fixes the day in the calendar forever: the tenth day of the seventh month. On it Israel must "afflict yourselves and... do no work" (v.29) — the one day of the year commanded for fasting and self-denial, a Sabbath of solemn rest. The people do nothing; the priest does everything; and "on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you" (v.30). It is to be repeated "once in the year... forever" — and that very repetition preaches its own insufficiency. A finished work is never repeated. That the Day of Atonement came round every autumn was God's annual reminder that the true and final atonement had not yet come.
verseByVerse.theology: The command to "afflict yourselves" and yet "do no work" holds two truths together: we bring nothing to our cleansing but our need, and we rest while Another works. Atonement is received, not achieved. Yet its yearly return exposes the shadow: "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins" (Heb 10:4). These sacrifices covered, deferred, and pointed forward; they could not finish. So the whole calendar leaned toward a cross, where One would cry "It is finished" (John 19:30) and the annual day would never be needed again.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every autumn Israel fasted, rested, and watched their high priest secure another year's cleansing — and then waited, because it would all have to be done again.

Now: our Day of Atonement is behind us, done once by the true High Priest, and it will never come round again. The believer's whole life becomes the Sabbath rest these verses foreshadowed: "we who have believed enter that rest" (Heb 4:3). We grieve our sin no longer to earn cleansing, but because we already have it; we rest, because He has worked.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work... For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest...
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the strange pairing: "afflict yourselves" and "do no work." Israel must feel the weight of sin — this was the one fast day in the law, a day to humble the soul — and yet must lift not a finger toward its own cleansing. Both are the gospel. We come empty-handed, mourning our sin, bringing nothing; and we rest, because the work is the priest's, not ours. "You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins" — not some, all; not partly, clean. What a word for a burdened conscience. And it is called "a Sabbath of solemn rest," the deepest rest of the year, because the deepest rest a soul can know is to be clean before God and to have contributed nothing but need. That rest has a name: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary... for the tent of meeting and for the altar... for the priests and for all the people of the assembly. And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: The atonement is total in its reach — sanctuary, tent, altar, priests, and "all the people of the assembly" — nothing and no one left uncleansed. Yet listen to the two words that expose the whole system's limit: "once in the year." Every autumn it came again, because every autumn it wore off. A finished work is never repeated; the yearly return of this day was God's own admission that the real atonement was still to come (Heb 10:1-4). And so the chapter that is the summit of Leviticus is also a signpost, pointing past itself to a hill outside Jerusalem where the true High Priest would enter the true sanctuary with His own blood, "once for all" (Heb 9:12), and sit down. The book closes its holiest chapter with "once in the year"; the gospel answers with "once for all." And the veil that kept us out was torn in two, from top to bottom, forever.

16.theology:
Propitiation. The blood on the mercy seat turns away wrath and satisfies justice. Christ is our hilasterion, the propitiation by his blood (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2) — the place where holiness and mercy meet.

Expiation. The scapegoat bears confessed sin away into the wilderness. Christ carries our sin beyond recovery: 'the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' (Isa 53:6).

Once for all. Aaron entered yearly with another's blood; Christ entered once with his own and sat down (Heb 9:12; 10:12). The torn veil (Matt 27:51) opens the way forever.
16.examples:
Then: Once a year all Israel waited in trembling silence as the high priest, in linen, passed alone through the veil with blood; one goat died and another was driven into the wilderness, and the nation was declared clean.

Now: Christ, our great High Priest, entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all. He is both the goat slain and the goat sent away. The veil is torn; we draw near with confidence (Heb 10:19-22), resting in his cry: 'It is finished.'

17.title: The Sanctity of Blood: Life Given for Life
17.text: <sup>11</sup>For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.
17.overview:
With chapter 17 we cross into the second half of Leviticus, often called the Holiness Code (chs 17–27), where the focus shifts from the sanctuary to the life of the people — holiness lived out in the world. And it begins, fittingly, with blood. All slaughter must be brought to the tabernacle; no sacrificing in the open field to demons; and above all, no eating of blood. Why such reverence for blood? The chapter gives the answer in the single most important verse for understanding atonement in all of Scripture.

"For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life" (17:11). Here is the theological key that unlocks the whole sacrificial system. Blood is life; the wages of sin is death; therefore atonement requires the giving of a life in the place of the forfeit life. The blood on the altar is not magic; it is substituted life. God himself says, "I have given it" — atonement is God's gift, God's provision, God's gracious appointment.

The writer of Hebrews builds his entire argument on this verse: "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22). There is no bloodless gospel. The cross is not an embarrassment to be explained away but the necessary outworking of this principle: life for life, blood for blood, the innocent for the guilty. To strip the blood from Christianity is to strip away the atonement, and with it all hope.

And the blood that once was forbidden to drink becomes, in Christ, the cup of the new covenant. "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:28). The blood of Christ "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24) — Abel's blood cried for vengeance; Christ's blood cries mercy, mercy, mercy. The sanctity of blood in Leviticus 17 finds its everlasting meaning at Calvary, where the life of the Son of God was poured out to make atonement for our souls.

sections.title: All Slaughter Brought to the LORD
sections.commentary:
Every animal killed for food must first be brought to the tabernacle, lest the people sacrifice "to goat demons, after whom they whore" (17:7). Calvin notes the pastoral wisdom: by centralizing slaughter, God guards his people from the idolatry that lurked in the open fields. Every meat-meal became an act of worship, a confession that life belongs to God.

The principle endures: there is no neutral territory. The God who claims the altar claims the field, the kitchen, the table. To take life, even for food, is to handle something sacred, and it must be done before the Lord.

sections.title: The Life Is in the Blood
sections.commentary:
This is the golden verse of Leviticus. "The life of the flesh is in the blood." Therefore blood, as life, is sacred — and therefore blood, as substituted life, can make atonement. Sproul called this the most concise statement of substitutionary atonement in the Old Testament. The penalty for sin is death; in the sacrificial blood, a life is given in the place of the sinner's life.

Note the divine initiative: "I have given it for you on the altar." Atonement is not something we achieve to placate an unwilling God; it is God's own gift, his gracious provision for our salvation. The cross is the Father's idea before it is the Son's obedience — "God so loved the world that he gave" (John 3:16). The blood does not change God's heart toward us; it flows from a heart already set on mercy.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Blood and Its Fulfillment
sections.commentary:
Twice the prohibition is pressed: no one shall eat blood, for the life is in it. The reverence is total. And this is what makes the words of Jesus at the Last Supper so staggering: "Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant" (Matt 26:27–28). The unthinkable command, the blood once utterly forbidden, now offered as the cup of salvation. In John 6 Jesus presses it to scandal: "unless you... drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53).

Begg observes the breathtaking reversal: the blood that meant death to consume now means life to receive — because it is the blood of the One whose life, poured out, becomes our life. "Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb 9:22), but the blood that has been shed now "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24), crying not for vengeance but for mercy over all who trust in Christ.

sections.title: Holiness in the Handling of Life
sections.commentary:
Even eating an animal that died of itself, with its blood undrained, brings uncleanness requiring washing. The reverence for blood extends to the edges of ordinary life. The lesson is cumulative: life is God's, blood is sacred, and the people of God must handle the gift of life with reverence and care.

For the church, the enduring application is a profound reverence for the blood of Christ. We dare not treat lightly what cost the Son of God his life. To trifle with sin is to trample the blood (Heb 10:29); to receive grace is to be awed by the price.

17.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. 'It is the blood that makes atonement by the life' (17:11) — the giving of a life in place of the forfeit life is the heart of the sacrificial system and the cross.

Atonement as God's gift. 'I have given it for you' — atonement is God's gracious provision, flowing from a heart already set on mercy (John 3:16).

The blood that speaks mercy. The blood once forbidden becomes the cup of the new covenant; Christ's blood 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel' (Heb 12:24).
17.examples:
Then: Israel brought all slaughter to the LORD and drained the blood, reverencing life as God's and learning that atonement comes only through substituted life.

Now: We rest in the blood of Christ, shed for the forgiveness of sins, and receive the cup of the new covenant with awe — for without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, and that blood has been shed for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands that all sacrifices be brought to the one altar at the tent of meeting — no more slaughtering in the open field, no more offerings to the "goat demons" after whom Israel had played the harlot. Worship is not to be improvised wherever a person pleases; it comes to God's appointed place, in God's appointed way. There is one altar, because there is one way to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Centralizing sacrifice at the one altar guards against idolatry ("goat demons," v.7) and against worship on human terms. It teaches that access to God is not a free-for-all but comes his way, at his appointed place — ultimately fulfilled in the one altar, the cross, and the one mediator, Christ, for "there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men" (1 Tim 2:5). There are not many ways to God; there is one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: an Israelite could not set up his own altar wherever he liked; he brought his offering to the one place God appointed.

Now: we do not invent our own way to God; we come by the one way he has opened — "no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). One altar, one Mediator, one gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat... and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD... that man shall be cut off from among his people... So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore.
verseByVerse.commentary: God commands that every sacrifice be brought to the one altar at the tent of meeting. No more killing sacrificial animals out in the open field, wherever one happened to be. Why such insistence on a single place? Two reasons surface. First, to guard against idolatry: scattered, private sacrifices had a way of drifting into offerings to "goat demons," the false gods of the field, "after whom they whore." Centralized worship kept Israel from slipping into the paganism all around them. Second, and deeper, to teach that worship comes to God on God's terms, at God's appointed place, in God's appointed way — never improvised to suit ourselves. There is one altar because there is one way to God. This truth runs straight through the Bible and lands at the cross, the one true altar, and at Christ, the one Mediator: "there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). The world imagines many roads up the mountain; God says there is one, and he has opened it himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-16 — The Life Is in the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now comes one of the most important verses in the entire Bible — the theological heart of the whole sacrificial system. God forbids the eating of blood, and tells them why: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life." Blood is sacred because life is sacred, and blood is the God-given means of atonement. Here, in one sentence, is why the cross had to be.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus 17:11 is the golden key to the whole book and to the gospel: "it is the blood that makes atonement by the life." Atonement requires the giving of a life, represented by blood, in the sinner's place — which is why "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22). Blood is not to be eaten because it is holy, God's appointed instrument of redemption. Every drop reverenced here points to "the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish" (1 Pet 1:19), the lifeblood that actually accomplishes what all these sacrifices foreshadowed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel reverenced blood as sacred, never consuming it, because it was God's appointed means of atonement for their souls.

Now: we live by the blood we could never earn: "you were ransomed... with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:18-19). The verse that forbade eating blood explains why the Lamb had to shed his.

verseByVerse.quote: If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person... For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.
verseByVerse.commentary: We have come to the golden verse of Leviticus, perhaps of the whole Old Testament sacrificial system. God forbids the eating of blood — and then, in explaining why, hands us the key that unlocks the meaning of every sacrifice in the book, and the cross itself: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life." Read that slowly. Why does atonement require blood? Because blood represents life, and the wages of sin is death (Rom 6:23). A life has been forfeited by sin; a life must be given to redeem it. The blood on the altar is a life laid down in the sinner's place. That is why blood is too sacred to be treated as food — it is God's own appointed instrument of redemption, holy beyond measure. And notice the astonishing grace in the words "I have given it for you." God himself provides the means of atonement; the sacrifice is his gift before it is our offering. This single verse is why the writer to the Hebrews can say, "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22), and why John the Baptist could point to Jesus and cry, "Behold, the Lamb of God" (John 1:29). Every reverenced drop of animal blood in Israel was a finger pointing forward to the precious blood of Christ, the one life given for our souls, the only blood that could ever truly make atonement.

18.title: Sexual Ethics: A People Called to Be Different
18.text: <sup>3</sup>You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you... <sup>4</sup>You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God.
18.overview:
Chapter 18 sets out the boundaries of sexual conduct, and its framework is everything. It opens and closes not with rules but with a Person: "I am the LORD your God" (18:2, 30). The sexual ethics of Israel are grounded in the character of God and the identity of his redeemed people. And the great refrain is the call to be different: "You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt... and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan" (18:3). Israel was redeemed out of one corrupt culture and brought toward another; in both, the surrounding world had made sexuality into idolatry. God calls his people to be holy, distinct, set apart even here — perhaps especially here.

The specific prohibitions guard the family, protect the vulnerable, honor the dignity of persons, and preserve the boundaries the Creator built into human life. These are not arbitrary taboos but the gracious fences around the garden of human flourishing. As Keller often argued, God's commands about sex are not the restrictions of a cosmic killjoy but the wisdom of a loving Maker who designed sexuality for covenant, faithfulness, and joy. To live outside the boundaries is not freedom but the slow defacing of the image of God.

The chapter is sobering in its warning that the land itself "vomited out" its previous inhabitants for these very practices (18:25), and that Israel risked the same. Sexual sin is never merely private; it defiles a people and provokes the holiness of God. Carson notes that few areas test a culture's submission to God more sharply than sexuality, where the pressure to conform to the surrounding world is fiercest.

For the church in every age, the call stands: be different. Do not do as the Egypt behind you or the Canaan before you. The gospel does not merely forbid; it transforms desire, dignifies the body as a temple of the Spirit (1 Cor 6:19), and points beyond every earthly union to the marriage of the Lamb. And for those who have failed — and who has not? — the same Christ who upholds the boundary also bore its breach, cleansing the worst sexual sinner who comes to him: "and such were some of you. But you were washed" (1 Cor 6:11).

sections.title: I Am the LORD Your God
sections.commentary:
The chapter is bracketed by God's self-identification. Before a single prohibition, God establishes the foundation: "I am the LORD your God" (18:2). Ethics flow from relationship; commands flow from covenant. Ferguson notes that biblical morality is never freestanding rule-keeping but the response of a redeemed people to their redeeming God.

"You shall not do as they do in Egypt... or in Canaan" (18:3). The people of God are summoned to nonconformity. Redeemed out of the world's corruption, they must not carry it with them nor adopt the corruption that lies ahead. "Do not be conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2) is the New Testament echo.

sections.title: The Boundaries of Sexual Conduct
sections.commentary:
The detailed prohibitions guard the integrity of the family and the dignity of persons. Incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, and other distortions are forbidden — practices common in the surrounding nations. Keller observed that God's design for sex within the covenant of marriage is not a cage but a garden; the boundaries exist to protect, not to deprive.

The mention of Molech (18:21) amid sexual sins is striking: the abuse of sexuality and the sacrifice of children are linked as twin profanations of life and the image of God. A culture that idolizes sex will, sooner or later, sacrifice its children. The holiness of God stands against every distortion of his gift.

sections.title: The Land Vomits Out Its Inhabitants
sections.commentary:
God warns that the Canaanites are being driven out precisely because of these practices, and that the land itself "vomited out its inhabitants" (18:25). Sexual sin is not a private matter; it defiles a people and a place. Sproul underscored that God's holiness is not indifferent to how we use our bodies; there are consequences woven into the moral fabric of creation.

Yet the warning is also mercy: God tells his people the danger so they may avoid it. And for those who have transgressed, the gospel offers what the law could not — cleansing. "Such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 6:11). The boundary that condemns is met by the blood that cleanses.

18.theology:
Holiness grounded in God. 'I am the LORD your God' brackets the chapter — sexual ethics flow from God's character and the identity of a redeemed people, not from arbitrary rule.

A people called to be different. Neither Egypt behind nor Canaan ahead is to shape God's people (18:3); the church is summoned to holy nonconformity (Rom 12:2).

The dignity of the body. God's boundaries protect persons and flourishing; in Christ the body becomes a temple of the Spirit (1 Cor 6:19), and even sexual sin is cleansed in him (1 Cor 6:11).
18.examples:
Then: Israel, surrounded by cultures that had made sex into idolatry, was called to honor God's boundaries and so to be visibly, holily different from Egypt and Canaan.

Now: The church faces the same fierce pressure to conform. We hold God's design as wisdom and gift, not cage — and we offer the cleansing of Christ to all who have failed, for 'you were washed.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-30 — Holiness in the Family and the Marriage Bed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God addresses the intimate life of his people — marriage, sexuality, and the family — and frames it with a command: "You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt... and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan." Israel is to be different. A long list of forbidden relations follows — incest, adultery, child sacrifice to Molech, homosexual acts, bestiality — and a solemn warning: these very sins so defiled the land of Canaan that it "vomited out" its inhabitants. God's people are to guard the God-given goodness of sex within its God-given bounds.
verseByVerse.theology: Sexuality is not a matter of indifference to God; it is a gift he designed, with boundaries that reflect his holiness (cf. Gen 2:24). The nations' practices — which Israel must refuse — defile not only individuals but the land itself (vv.24-28). The New Testament echoes these very standards (1 Cor 6:9-11; Rom 1:24-27), yet always with gospel hope: "and such were some of you. But you were washed... sanctified... justified" (1 Cor 6:11). God's word here is not the cold voice of a killjoy but the loving boundary of a Father who knows that sex, kept holy, is a blessing, and sex unmoored becomes a ruin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: surrounded by Egypt's and Canaan's practices, Israel was called to a radically different sexual holiness — reflecting God's design amid a watching, corrupted world.

Now: the boundaries still stand, and so does the grace: whatever our past, in Christ we are "washed... sanctified... justified" (1 Cor 6:11). God's design for our bodies is not a cage but a shelter, and his mercy meets every failure.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not do as they do in the land of Egypt, where you lived, and you shall not do as they do in the land of Canaan, to which I am bringing you. You shall not walk in their statutes. You shall follow my rules and keep my statutes and walk in them. I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before a single specific command, God sets the frame, and it is all about identity and belonging. "You shall not do as they do in Egypt... you shall not do as they do in Canaan." Israel lived between two cultures — the one they came out of and the one they were going into — and both were saturated with practices God's people must refuse. The reason is not that God is against pleasure or that sex is dirty; the very opposite. It is that his people belong to him and are to reflect his character in the most intimate corners of life. "I am the LORD your God" — that is the ground of every rule that follows. Holiness is not first a list of prohibitions but a relationship: you are mine, so live like it. And notice how God says his ways are the path of life: "if a person does them, he shall live by them" (v.5). God's boundaries around sexuality are not a fence to keep us from joy, but the banks of a river that keep its waters from becoming a destructive flood.

verseByVerse.quote: None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD... You shall not lie with a male as with a woman; it is an abomination. And you shall not lie with any animal and so make yourself unclean by it... You shall not give any of your children to offer them to Molech.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the specific prohibitions, and they are sobering: relations within the family (incest in its many forms), adultery, homosexual acts, bestiality, and — chillingly placed among the sexual sins — the sacrifice of children to the god Molech. These were not abstract dangers; they were the ordinary practices of the surrounding nations, woven into their religion. God draws a bright, clear line. We should read these verses without flinching and without cruelty. God is not sneering at people; he is guarding the goodness of what he made. Sexuality is his gift, designed for the covenant union of husband and wife (Gen 2:24), and every boundary here protects that gift from being twisted into something that wounds. The New Testament does not soften these standards (1 Cor 6:9-11; Rom 1:24-27), but it never leaves them as bare law. After listing such sins, Paul adds the sweetest words: "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 6:11). The law names the sin; the gospel washes the sinner. No one who comes to Christ is beyond his cleansing, whatever the past.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not make yourselves unclean by any of these things, for by all these the nations I am driving out before you have become unclean, and the land became unclean, so that I punished its iniquity, and the land vomited out its inhabitants... lest the land vomit you out when you make it unclean, as it vomited out the nation that was before you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God closes with a grave warning that lifts these commands above mere private morality. The sins just named did not only defile individuals; they defiled the very land, so that Canaan "vomited out" its inhabitants. And the same fate threatens Israel if they imitate them. This is startling and important: sexual sin is never merely a private choice with no wider effect. It corrupts families, communities, whole cultures; it pollutes the land itself. God takes it that seriously because he takes his people, and their witness among the nations, that seriously. There is a sober realism here that our age needs to hear: what a society celebrates in the bedroom eventually reshapes the whole society, for better or worse. Yet even this warning is mercy — God tells Israel plainly, before they enter the land, what will preserve them and what will destroy them, because he wants them to live. His commands are the loving guardrails of a Father who has watched a whole civilization ruin itself, and does not want his children to follow.

19.title: The Holiness Code: Love Your Neighbor
19.text: <sup>2</sup>Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy... <sup>18</sup>You shall not take vengeance or bear a grudge against the sons of your own people, but you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
19.overview:
If chapter 16 is the theological summit of Leviticus, chapter 19 is its ethical heart. It opens with the book's defining command — "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2) — and then, astonishingly, shows what that holiness looks like not in the sanctuary but on the street, in the field, in the marketplace, in the way you treat the deaf, the blind, the poor, the foreigner, and your own neighbor. Holiness, it turns out, is intensely practical and profoundly social.

This chapter weaves together echoes of the Ten Commandments with a stream of vivid social ethics: leave the gleanings of your field for the poor and the sojourner (19:9–10, the law that fed Ruth); do not oppress your worker or withhold his wages overnight (19:13); do not curse the deaf or trip the blind (19:14); use honest weights and measures (19:35–36); show respect to the elderly (19:32). True holiness is not a withdrawal from the world into religious privacy; it is the love of God spilling over into the love of neighbor.

And at the center stands the verse Jesus would lift up as the second great commandment: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD" (19:18). When asked to summarize the whole law, our Lord reached into Leviticus 19 (Matt 22:39). Paul too: "the whole law is fulfilled in one word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself'" (Gal 5:14). The Holiness Code, so often dismissed as ancient ritual, contains the very command that crowns Christian ethics.

Carson notes how the chapter refuses to separate worship and ethics, the vertical and the horizontal. "I am the LORD" punctuates the chapter like a drumbeat, grounding every social command in the character of God. To love your neighbor is to be like God; to cheat the poor is to deny him. And the One who gave this law also kept it perfectly — Jesus, the true neighbor, who loved not himself but us, who became poor that we might be rich, and who pours his own self-giving love into our hearts by the Spirit so that we, made holy, might love as we have been loved.

sections.title: Be Holy, for I Am Holy
sections.commentary:
The chapter's keynote sounds at once: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2). Strikingly, what immediately follows are echoes of the commandments — reverence for parents, keeping the Sabbath, rejecting idols. Ferguson notes that holiness is here defined by likeness to God's character, expressed in obedience to his Word.

Holiness is not first an emotion or an experience but a way of life conformed to God's revealed will. And it is addressed to "all the congregation" — not a spiritual elite but the whole people of God. Every believer is called to be holy.

sections.title: Holiness on the Street: Justice for the Poor and Vulnerable
sections.commentary:
Now holiness descends to the field and the marketplace. Leave the gleanings for the poor and the sojourner (19:9–10) — the very law under which Ruth gathered grain in Boaz's field, the law that would feed the great-grandmother of David and the ancestress of Christ. Do not steal, lie, oppress, or withhold wages (19:11–13). Do not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind (19:14) — protect those who cannot protect themselves.

And then the summit: "you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD" (19:18). Jesus called this the second greatest commandment (Matt 22:39); Paul said the whole law is fulfilled in it (Gal 5:14). Keller observed that biblical love is not mere sentiment but costly, practical action for the good of the neighbor — the very love God showed us in Christ. Holiness and love are not rivals; love is the shape holiness takes among people.

sections.title: Honest Weights and Reverent Living
sections.commentary:
The chapter continues with a tapestry of commands: respect for the elderly (19:32), love for the sojourner as for oneself (19:34), and honest weights and measures (19:35–36). "You shall have just balances, just weights" — for God himself is just, and his people must reflect his justice in the smallest commercial transaction. Calvin notes that to cheat with weights is to deny the God who sees, dishonesty being a form of practical atheism.

The repeated refrain "I am the LORD" grounds it all. Every command, however small, is rooted in the character of God. To be holy is to be like him — just, generous, truthful, protective of the weak — in every corner of ordinary life. This is the comprehensive vision of a holy community, and it finds its fulfillment in the Spirit-filled church that loves as Christ loved.

19.theology:
Practical holiness. 'Be holy, for I am holy' (19:2) is worked out not in ritual withdrawal but in justice, generosity, honesty, and love on the street and in the field.

Love your neighbor. The command Jesus crowned as second greatest (Matt 22:39; 19:18) and Paul called the law's fulfillment (Gal 5:14) sits at the heart of the Holiness Code.

'I am the LORD.' The repeated refrain grounds all ethics in God's character; to love the neighbor and deal justly is to be like God himself.
19.examples:
Then: An Israelite farmer left the edges of his field unharvested for the poor, paid his workers promptly, used honest scales, and loved his neighbor — and in such mundane mercy, reflected the holiness of God.

Now: Holiness still wears work clothes. We honor God in how we treat employees, the vulnerable, the elderly, and the stranger — loving our neighbor as ourselves because Christ first loved us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-37 — 'You Shall Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the beating heart of the Holiness Code, and one of the richest chapters in the law. It opens with the theme of the whole book — "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" — and then shows what holiness actually looks like on the ground: honoring parents, keeping Sabbath, leaving the edges of your field for the poor, paying wages on time, not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind, judging justly, and — at its summit — "you shall love your neighbor as yourself." Holiness here is not retreat from the world into ritual; it is love made practical, woven through daily life.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus 19 shows that holiness and love are one: to be holy as God is holy (v.2) is to love your neighbor as yourself (v.18) — the verse Jesus called the second great commandment (Matt 22:39) and Paul called the fulfilling of the law (Rom 13:9; Gal 5:14). The refrain "I am the LORD" punctuates the chapter dozens of times, grounding every ethical command in the character of God himself. Notice that love is concrete: it is gleaning laws for the poor (vv.9-10), prompt wages (v.13), care for the disabled (v.14), honest courts (v.15), even love for the sojourner "as yourself" (v.34). This is the holiness that took flesh in Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: holiness meant a farmer leaving grain in the corners for the poor, an employer paying the day laborer before nightfall, a judge refusing to favor rich or poor — love with work boots on.

Now: "you shall love your neighbor as yourself" is still the shape of holiness (Matt 22:39). Real godliness is not merely felt or professed; it is paid, given, and done — to the poor, the worker, the stranger, the neighbor.

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. Every one of you shall revere his mother and his father, and you shall keep my Sabbaths: I am the LORD your God. Do not turn to idols...
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with the theme verse of all Leviticus, now spoken not just to priests but to "all the congregation": "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy." Every Israelite, not just the professionals of religion, is called to reflect God's own character. And immediately the chapter shows that this holiness is deeply practical and, strikingly, echoes the Ten Commandments in fresh order — revere your mother and father, keep the Sabbath, turn from idols. Holiness begins at home and in worship: honoring those God set over us, resting in trust, refusing every rival to God. Notice how the command "revere your mother and father" puts the mother first here — a quiet dignity given to her that the ancient world often withheld. From its very first lines, this chapter tells us that being holy is not about escaping ordinary life into special religious acts. It is about letting the character of a holy God shape the most ordinary relationships and rhythms of every single day.

verseByVerse.quote: When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field right up to its edge... you shall leave them for the poor and for the sojourner... You shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him. The wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night until the morning... you shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now watch holiness put on work boots. It looks like a farmer deliberately not harvesting the corners of his field, leaving grain and grapes for the poor and the immigrant to gather with dignity — the very law under which Ruth would one day glean (Ruth 2). It looks like paying the day laborer his wages before nightfall, because he needs to feed his family tonight, not next week. It looks like refusing to curse the deaf (who cannot hear you) or trip the blind (who cannot see it coming) — kindness even when no one would ever know. It looks like courts that will not favor the rich or the poor but judge with truth. And it rises, at last, to the summit of the whole chapter, indeed of the whole law: "you shall love your neighbor as yourself." Jesus himself lifted this single verse out of Leviticus 19 and called it the second greatest commandment, on which "depend all the Law and the Prophets" (Matt 22:39-40); Paul said it fulfills the whole law (Rom 13:9). Here, buried in the middle of Leviticus, is the golden rule of God's heart. And notice: biblical love is never a mere warm feeling. It is grain left in the field, wages paid on time, justice done, the vulnerable protected. Love with hands and feet — that is what holiness looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall keep my statutes... You shall not eat any flesh with the blood in it... When a stranger sojourns with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself... You shall have just balances, just weights... I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter continues to weave holiness through every thread of life — laws about crops and clothing, warnings against pagan practices like divination and the mutilations of mourning, calls to honor the elderly ("You shall stand up before the gray head," v.32) and to use honest weights and measures in business. Some of these commands are tied to Israel's particular calling and time; others voice timeless principles. But two shine especially bright. First, the sojourner: "you shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt" (vv.33-34). The command to love your neighbor is explicitly stretched to include the outsider, the immigrant, the one not like you — grounded, again, in Israel's own memory of being strangers. Second, honest weights: God cares whether your business scales are rigged, because holiness reaches into the marketplace, not just the sanctuary. Threading it all together, over and over, is the refrain "I am the LORD." Every command, great and small, rests on the same foundation: the character of the God who redeemed them. Holiness, in the end, is simply living all of life — harvest, wages, courts, business, the way we treat the old and the outsider — in the presence and the likeness of a holy God.

20.title: Penalties for Violations: The Seriousness of Sin
20.text: <sup>7</sup>Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God... <sup>26</sup>You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 returns to many of the sins named in chapter 18 — child sacrifice to Molech, occult practices, sexual transgressions — but now attaches penalties, often capital. To modern readers this is among the most difficult chapters in the Bible, and we must read it with both honesty and care. It reveals, with unflinching seriousness, how gravely God regards sin within his covenant community.

We must remember the unique situation: Israel was a theocracy, a nation under the direct rule of God, set apart to be the people through whom the Messiah would come and the holiness of God would be displayed to the nations. The severity of the penalties reflects the holiness of the God who dwelt in their midst and the cosmic stakes of preserving the line of promise. Sproul reminds us that our discomfort with these penalties often exposes how lightly we take sin, not how harshly God takes it. The wonder of grace can only be felt against the backdrop of sin's true seriousness.

Yet the chapter is not finally about death; it is about holiness and belonging. It opens and closes with the call to consecration: "Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy" (20:7), and "You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine" (20:26). The penalties serve this end — the formation of a people set apart, distinct, holy, belonging wholly to God.

And here the gospel shines through the severity. The law shows that sin deserves death — and it does, for "the wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23). But the One who gave the law also fulfilled its sentence in our place. Every capital penalty in this chapter is a shadow of the death we deserved; and Christ bore that death, becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13), so that we who deserved to be cut off might instead be made holy and brought near. The chapter that pronounces death over sin drives us to the cross, where death was swallowed up in the death of the Son, and where God's people are at last made truly his.

sections.title: Against Molech and the Occult
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with the most horrifying sin: giving children to Molech (20:2–5). The God of life stands implacably against the sacrifice of children, and against the occult attempts to seek power and knowledge apart from him (20:6). These are not mere ceremonial infractions but assaults on the image of God and the lordship of God.

The call to "consecrate yourselves... and be holy" (20:7) frames the whole. Sproul noted that God's severity toward these sins is the measure of his holiness and his love for the vulnerable. A God indifferent to the murder of children would not be holy or good.

sections.title: The Penalties and the Holiness of God
sections.commentary:
The catalog of penalties is sobering. Within the theocracy, certain sins carried capital consequences, for they struck at the very foundations of the covenant community and the line of promise. Carson cautions against two errors: minimizing the seriousness of sin, and importing these civil penalties directly into the church age, which is not a theocracy but lives under the gospel of grace and the discipline of the Spirit.

What endures is the lesson that sin is deadly serious to God. Our age, which treats sin as a minor inconvenience or a medical condition, desperately needs to recover the weight Leviticus gives it. Only when we feel the death that sin deserves can we marvel at the life that grace gives.

sections.title: Separated to Be His Own
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes where Leviticus always returns: holiness and belonging. "You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine" (20:26). The penalties served this glorious end — a people set apart, distinct from the nations, belonging wholly to God.

Begg loves the phrase "that you should be mine." The whole point of separation is possession — God claiming a people for his own treasured possession. Peter applies it to the church: "a people for his own possession" (1 Pet 2:9). And what the law could only command, Christ accomplishes: he "gave himself for us to redeem us... and to purify for himself a people for his own possession" (Titus 2:14). We are made holy and made his, not by keeping the penalties but by the One who bore them.

20.theology:
The seriousness of sin. The capital penalties reveal how gravely God regards sin in his covenant community; 'the wages of sin is death' (Rom 6:23). Our discomfort exposes how lightly we take sin.

Theocracy, not the church. These civil penalties belonged to Israel's unique theocracy; the church lives under grace and the discipline of the Spirit, not the sword.

Separated to be his own. 'You shall be holy to me... that you should be mine' (20:26) — fulfilled as Christ purifies 'a people for his own possession' (Titus 2:14).
20.examples:
Then: Israel learned, through severe penalties, that sin against a holy God is deadly serious, and that they were a people separated from the nations to belong wholly to him.

Now: We do not wield Israel's civil sword, but we recover sin's true weight — and we marvel that Christ bore the death we deserved, that we who deserved to be cut off are made holy and made his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-27 — Penalties, and a People Set Apart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If chapter 18 named the corruptions Israel must avoid, chapter 20 attaches the penalties — and they are severe. Giving children to Molech, consulting mediums, cursing parents, adultery, incest, homosexual acts, bestiality: these carry the gravest consequences in Israel's law. The severity measures the seriousness of the sin and the holiness of the God at the center of the camp. And through it all runs the refrain that explains everything: "You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy, and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine."
verseByVerse.theology: These are the civil penalties of the theocracy of Israel, a nation uniquely called to embody God's holiness in the land where his sanctuary stood — they are not a template for the church, which wields no sword but disciplines by exclusion, not execution (1 Cor 5:5; cf. John 8:11). What they reveal is the true wages of sin: "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezek 18:20), "the wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23). The gospel does not deny this death sentence; it announces that Christ bore it in our place (Gal 3:13). And the chapter's ground note — "I have separated you... that you should be mine" (v.26) — is pure grace: holiness flows from belonging to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the deadly penalties taught Israel that sin among God's people, near God's dwelling, is no light thing — it defiles, and it kills.

Now: we deserved the death these laws pronounce, but "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Gal 3:13). We are set apart, not by our own purity, but because he made us his own (v.26).

verseByVerse.quote: Any one of the people of Israel... who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death... I myself will set my face against that man and will cut him off from among his people, because he has given one of his children to Molech, to make my sanctuary unclean and to profane my holy name... Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy, for I am the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter opens with the most horrifying sin of all: giving children to Molech, the fire-god of the nations, by burning them alive in sacrifice. God's response is white-hot: "I myself will set my face against that man." This is not cold legalism; it is a Father's fury at the murder of children in the name of religion. And notice why God says it is so grave: it "makes my sanctuary unclean" and "profanes my holy name." Sin among God's people, so near his dwelling, is not a private matter — it defiles the holy place and drags his name through the mud. Yet even here, in a chapter of penalties, grace sounds: "Consecrate yourselves, therefore, and be holy." God does not merely threaten; he calls his people upward, to reflect the holiness of the God who has claimed them. Judgment on sin and the call to holiness are two sides of the same love — a love that will not leave his people to be destroyed by the very evils that destroyed the nations before them.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death... If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death... You shall keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the penalties for the sins named in chapter 18 — and they are the gravest in Israel's law, most carrying the death penalty. We must read these rightly. This was the civil law of a unique nation, a theocracy where God himself was King and his holy sanctuary stood in the center of the camp; the purity of the whole people, in the very presence of God, was at stake. These penalties are not handed to the church, which does not wield the sword. When a woman caught in adultery was dragged before Jesus, he did not stone her; he said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more" (John 8:11). And when the church faces grave sin, its weapon is not execution but loving exclusion, aimed at restoration (1 Cor 5:5). So what do these fierce penalties teach us? They teach the true weight of sin. What we treat lightly, God weighs as death, for "the wages of sin is death" (Rom 6:23). These verses hold up a mirror to show us what we all deserve. And that is exactly what makes the gospel so staggering: the death sentence these laws pronounce fell, in full, on Christ. "He became a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), so that we who deserved to be cut off might be brought near.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall therefore keep all my statutes and all my rules and do them, that the land where I am bringing you to live may not vomit you out... You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends by lifting our eyes from the penalties to the purpose behind them all: "You shall be holy to me, for I the LORD am holy and have separated you from the peoples, that you should be mine." There it is, the golden thread. Why all these commands, all these boundaries, all this seriousness about sin? Because God has set Israel apart to be his own treasured possession, and a people who belong to a holy God must look like him. Hear the tenderness underneath the holiness: "that you should be mine." This is not a distant deity issuing arbitrary rules; it is a God who has claimed a people for himself and wants them to flourish as his own, distinct from the corrupt and self-destroying nations around them. And this is the ground of all Christian holiness too. We are not made holy in order to become God's; we are holy because we already are his, "a people for his own possession" (1 Pet 2:9). He separated us to himself by the blood of his Son. Now we live set apart — not to earn his love, but because we are already, gloriously, his.

21.title: Holiness for the Priests: A Higher Standard
21.text: <sup>6</sup>They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God... <sup>8</sup>You shall sanctify him... He shall be holy to you, for I, the LORD, who sanctify you, am holy.
21.overview:
Chapters 21 and 22 raise the standard for those who draw nearest to God — the priests. If the whole nation is called to be holy, the priests are called to a holiness yet more exacting, for they handle the holy things and stand in the gap between God and the people. To whom much is given, much is required. The closer one comes to the consuming fire, the more careful one must be.

The priests must guard themselves from defilement by the dead (21:1–4), must not disfigure themselves in pagan mourning rites (21:5), must marry with care (21:7), and the high priest above all must keep himself wholly undefiled (21:10–15). Most striking, no priest with a physical blemish may approach the altar to offer the bread of his God (21:17–23) — not as a judgment on his worth, but as a living parable: the one who serves the perfect God must himself be a picture of wholeness and perfection.

This points unmistakably to Christ, our Great High Priest. Where Aaron's sons were barred for blemishes of the body, and even the high priest needed cleansing for his own sin, Jesus is the priest who is "holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens" (Heb 7:26). He is the flawless priest the law required but Aaron could never be — without sin, without blemish, without the defilement of death (which he conquered), fit to enter the true sanctuary and offer the perfect sacrifice, which was himself.

And here is the grace that turns the chapter inside out for us: the unblemished requirement that disqualified the blemished priest now qualifies us, for our standing rests not on our own wholeness but on Christ's. The blemished are not barred from God in the new covenant; the lame, the blind, the broken are welcomed at the feast (Luke 14:21). For the spotless Priest has clothed us in his own perfection, and in him even we — blemished, halting, scarred — are made priests to our God (1 Pet 2:9).

sections.title: The Priests Set Apart from Defilement
sections.commentary:
The ordinary priest must avoid contact with the dead except for close family (21:1–4) and must not adopt the self-mutilating mourning customs of the pagans (21:5). "They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God" (21:6). The priest's life, public and private, reflects on the holiness of the God he serves.

Calvin observes that those who handle holy things bear a weighty responsibility, for their conduct either honors or profanes God's name before the people. The principle endures for all who lead in God's church: a higher standard, a closer walk, a greater accountability (James 3:1; 1 Tim 3).

sections.title: The High Priest's Greater Holiness
sections.commentary:
The high priest, anointed and clothed in the holy garments, must keep himself even more strictly — not defiling himself even for his own father or mother (21:11), not leaving the sanctuary in mourning. He bears the holiness of God in concentrated form.

Ferguson draws the line to Christ: every restriction on Aaron is a shadow of the unblemished perfection of Jesus. The high priest who could not be defiled by death points to the One who entered death itself and was not defiled but conquered it, rising to enter the heavenly sanctuary as our eternal High Priest.

sections.title: No Blemish at the Altar
sections.commentary:
No descendant of Aaron with a physical defect may approach to offer the bread of his God (21:17–23). This is not contempt for the disabled — such a priest still eats the holy food (21:22) — but a vivid symbol: the service of the perfect God must picture perfection. The blemish in the priest, like the blemish forbidden in the sacrifice, teaches that nothing flawed can stand in the place of mediation.

And so we are driven to Christ, "a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19) and a priest "holy, innocent, unstained" (Heb 7:26) — at once the flawless sacrifice and the flawless priest. Begg marvels at the reversal of the new covenant: in Christ, the blemished are welcomed, the broken are brought near, and the very ones the old law would bar are made priests to God, clothed in a perfection not their own.

21.theology:
A higher standard for leaders. Those who draw nearest to God bear greater accountability; the closer to the holy fire, the more careful one must be (James 3:1).

The unblemished priest. The demand for a flawless priest and sacrifice points to Christ, 'holy, innocent, unstained' (Heb 7:26), the spotless Lamb (1 Pet 1:19).

Grace for the blemished. In Christ the broken are welcomed and made priests, clothed in his perfection — the very ones the old law would have barred (Luke 14:21; 1 Pet 2:9).
21.examples:
Then: Israel's priests, and the high priest above all, kept a stricter holiness, and no blemished descendant of Aaron approached the altar — a living parable that the perfect God must be served with pictures of perfection.

Now: We rest in Christ, the flawless High Priest and spotless Lamb, who clothes us blemished sinners in his own perfection and makes us priests to our God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-24 — The Holiness of the Priests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Holiness is required of all Israel, but even more of the priests who serve at the altar. God gives special rules for them — about mourning, marriage, and physical wholeness — and stricter rules still for the high priest. Those who handle holy things must themselves be marked by holiness. A priest with a bodily defect may not offer the sacrifices, though — tenderly — he still eats the holy food. All of it points to the one perfect Priest who was without any blemish at all.
verseByVerse.theology: The higher the calling, the higher the standard: the priests, and above all the high priest, must be holy "because they offer the LORD's food offerings" (v.6). The requirement of physical wholeness (vv.17-23) was a visible parable of the inward, moral perfection required to approach God — and it points to Christ, our High Priest, "holy, innocent, unstained" (Heb 7:26), the unblemished Lamb (1 Pet 1:19). Yet grace glimmers even here: the disabled priest still "may eat the bread of his God" (v.22) — excluded from serving, but never from the table. And in Christ, the very blind and lame David's men scorned are welcomed in (cf. 2 Sam 5:8; Luke 14:21).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priest who served God had to be marked out by holiness and wholeness — a living picture of the perfection required to draw near.

Now: we come through a High Priest who is perfectly holy and without blemish (Heb 7:26), and in him even the broken and the outcast — all of us — are welcomed to the table of God (Luke 14:21-23).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron... None of them shall make himself unclean for the dead among his people, except for his closest relatives... They shall be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: God now raises the bar for those who serve him most closely. The priests are held to stricter standards than ordinary Israelites — even in how they mourn the dead (which brings ceremonial uncleanness) and whom they marry. Why the extra weight? The text says it plainly: "For they offer the LORD's food offerings, the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy." The nearer a person stands to the holy things of God, the more his life must match his calling. This is a principle that runs right through Scripture and lands on the church: "Not many of you should become teachers... for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness" (James 3:1). Leadership in the things of God is not a privilege to be flaunted but a holiness to be lived. Those who handle sacred things, who represent God to his people, carry a heavier responsibility to be what they proclaim. The pulpit and the altar demand not perfection of gifting but genuine, visible holiness of life.

verseByVerse.quote: The priest who is chief among his brothers, on whose head the anointing oil is poured and who has been consecrated to wear the garments, shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes... He shall take as his wife a virgin... that he may not profane his offspring among his people.
verseByVerse.commentary: Stricter still are the rules for the high priest, the one man who would enter the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. He must not even mourn with the ordinary signs of grief, not for his own father or mother, because he bears the anointing oil of God upon him and must not leave the sanctuary. His marriage, too, is guarded. Everything about him is to speak of undivided consecration to God. He is set apart in the most complete way, a living emblem of holiness. And of course he points beyond himself. Every rule that fenced the high priest with holiness was a shadow cast backward by the true High Priest, Jesus, who is "holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners" (Heb 7:26). Aaron and his successors had to be made holy by oil and rules and endless care; Christ was holy in his very being, and entered the true sanctuary not with the blood of goats but with his own, once for all (Heb 9:12). The high priest's consecration was real, but partial and outward; in Jesus, at last, the reality came.

verseByVerse.quote: None of your offspring throughout their generations who has a blemish may approach to offer the bread of his God... For no one who has a blemish shall draw near... But he may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things. Only he shall not go through the veil...
verseByVerse.commentary: Finally, a rule that can trouble tender hearts: a priest with a physical defect — blind, lame, disfigured — may not offer the sacrifices. We must understand this rightly. It is not that God despises the disabled; he made them, loves them, and defends them (19:14). Rather, physical wholeness in the priest was a visible parable of the moral and spiritual perfection required to approach a holy God. The unblemished priest, like the unblemished lamb, pointed to a perfection none of us possesses in ourselves. And here is the tender grace tucked into the very same law: the priest with a blemish "may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy things." He is not cast out, not left to starve, not treated as worthless. He may not serve at the altar, but he is fully fed at God's table. And this is where the gospel shines brightest. The law required an unblemished priest, and we had none — until Christ, the one truly without blemish, came and served in our place. And now, because of him, the very blind and lame who could not draw near are carried right in: "Bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame," says the Master of the feast (Luke 14:21). The perfect Priest opens the table to the imperfect. What the law kept back, grace brings home.

22.title: Holy Offerings: Nothing Blemished for God
22.text: <sup>20</sup>You shall not offer anything that has a blemish, for it will not be acceptable for you. <sup>21</sup>...to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 continues the theme of holiness, turning from the holiness of the priests to the holiness of the offerings they handle and the requirement that every sacrifice be without blemish. The priests must not eat the holy food while unclean (22:1–9); only those belonging to the priestly household may share it (22:10–16); and every animal offered to the LORD must be perfect, "without blemish" (22:17–25).
