God will not be honored with the maimed, the diseased, the leftover, or the second-rate.

The repeated insistence — "to be accepted it must be perfect; there shall be no blemish in it" (22:21) — is one of the great refrains of the sacrificial system, and it sets the standard that no earthly lamb could ultimately meet. For even the finest, most flawless animal in Israel's flocks was still only an animal, unable truly to take away sin. The demand for perfection points beyond every spotless lamb to the one perfect Lamb.

Malachi would later thunder against priests who broke this very law, offering blind and lame animals to God: "When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil?... Present that to your governor; will he accept you?" (Mal 1:8). To give God less than our best is to despise his name. And Begg presses the searching question to our own hearts: do we give God the firstfruits or the leftovers? The prime of our strength or the dregs of our exhaustion?

But the chapter's deepest note is gospel. The unblemished offering finds its fulfillment in Christ, "a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19), who alone met the standard the law demanded. He is the perfect sacrifice God required and the perfect sacrifice God provided. Where every Israelite searched his flock for a flawless lamb, God searched all heaven and earth and provided his own Son. The Lamb of God is the only offering ever truly "without blemish" — and in him, our imperfect worship is made acceptable.

sections.title: Holy Things Handled in Holiness
sections.commentary:
The priests must treat the holy offerings with reverence, not eating them while ceremonially unclean (22:3–9), lest they "profane my holy name" (22:2). Only the priestly household may partake (22:10–13). Holy things are not common; they must be handled with care befitting the God to whom they belong.

The principle carries forward: those who handle the holy things of God — the Word, the sacraments, the worship of the church — must do so with reverence and a clean conscience. Calvin warns against the casual familiarity that breeds contempt for sacred things.

sections.title: Without Blemish: The Standard of Acceptance
sections.commentary:
Here is the heart of the chapter: every offering must be "without blemish" to be accepted (22:20–21). No blind, injured, maimed, or diseased animal may be brought (22:22). God demands the best, the whole, the perfect. To offer less is to insult the Giver of all.

This standard, impossible for sinful worshippers to satisfy at the deepest level, points to Christ. Peter deliberately echoes it: we are ransomed "with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19). The flawless animal foreshadowed the flawless Savior. And Malachi's rebuke of those who gave God their worst (Mal 1:8) still searches us: God is worthy of our best, our first, our finest — yet our best is acceptable only in the truly spotless Lamb.

sections.title: I Am the LORD Who Sanctifies
sections.commentary:
The chapter closes with the recurring ground of all holiness: "I am the LORD who sanctifies you, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God" (22:32–33). It is God who makes holy. Holiness is not first our achievement but his gift and his work; we are sanctified by the LORD who redeemed us.

Ferguson highlights the gospel order: redemption first ("brought you out of Egypt"), then sanctification ("who sanctifies you"). The God who saves is the God who makes holy. And in the new covenant, this is the Spirit's work, applying the perfect offering of Christ so that we, sanctified, are made acceptable to God in the Beloved.

22.theology:
Without blemish. The demand for a flawless offering (22:21) sets a standard no earthly lamb could ultimately meet, pointing to Christ, 'a lamb without blemish or spot' (1 Pet 1:19).

God deserves our best. To offer the maimed or leftover is to despise God's name (Mal 1:8); he is worthy of our first and finest.

The LORD who sanctifies. 'I am the LORD who sanctifies you' (22:32) — holiness is God's gift and work, grounded in redemption and applied by the Spirit.
22.examples:
Then: An Israelite searched his flock for a flawless animal, for God would accept no blemished offering; the priests handled the holy things with clean reverence.

Now: We bring God our best, not our leftovers — yet we rest our acceptance not on our flawed offerings but on the one spotless Lamb, in whom even our imperfect worship is made acceptable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives careful rules about the priests eating the holy portions of the offerings: they must be clean to do so, and no outsider may share in what is holy. To treat the sacred carelessly is to "profane" God's holy name. Even the privilege of the priest's table is hedged with reverence — holy things are to be handled as holy.
verseByVerse.theology: The repeated concern that the priests "not profane my holy name" (v.2) by careless handling of holy things teaches reverence — familiarity with sacred things must never breed contempt. Only the clean may partake, and only those who belong (vv.10-13); the holy is not common property. It warns all who serve God against treating the sacred casually (cf. 1 Cor 11:27-29), and magnifies the seriousness of the God whose name is holy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the priest could eat the holy food only when clean, and no stranger could share it — the sacred kept sacred.

Now: those who handle holy things — the Word, the Table, the name of God — must never grow casual with them. "Let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe" (Heb 12:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Speak to Aaron and his sons so that they abstain from the holy things of the people of Israel, which they dedicate to me, so that they do not profane my holy name... An outsider shall not eat of a holy thing... If anyone eats of a holy thing unintentionally, he shall add the fifth of its value to it and give the holy thing to the priest.
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses guard the holy portions of the offerings — the food God assigned to the priests — with careful rules. A priest must be ceremonially clean to eat them; no outsider, not even a priest's guest or hired servant, may share in what is holy; and to eat a holy thing wrongly requires restitution. Running through it all is one anxious concern: that the priests "do not profane my holy name." The danger for those who live closest to sacred things is that the sacred becomes ordinary to them. Handle the holy every day, and you can begin to treat it as common. God will not have it so. The very privilege of the priest's table is fenced with reverence, precisely because familiarity so easily breeds contempt. There is a searching word here for everyone who serves God — pastors, teachers, all who handle his Word and his Table week by week. The things of God are never to be treated casually. Paul warned the Corinthians against coming carelessly to the Lord's Supper (1 Cor 11:27-29). May we never let our nearness to holy things dull our awe of the holy God, but "offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe" (Heb 12:28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the offerings themselves: they must be "without blemish," male, whole, perfect — nothing blind, injured, maimed, or defective may be brought to God. To offer the leftovers, the second-rate, the animal you would not want yourself, is to insult the God who gave you everything. God is worthy of the best. And every spotless offering points to the one truly unblemished Lamb.
verseByVerse.theology: "It must be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish in it" (v.21) — God will not receive our leftovers and rejects. Malachi thunders against exactly this profanation: offering the blind and lame, "what your governor would not accept" (Mal 1:8). The demand for an unblemished sacrifice points to "a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19), Christ, the only offering truly perfect, whom God accepted in full on our behalf. In him we now give our best in glad response, not to earn acceptance but because we are accepted.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the worshiper had to bring an unblemished animal, not the sickly one he could spare — God is honored with the best, not the leftovers.

Now: God still deserves our first and finest — time, money, strength — not the scraps. And our confidence rests on the one unblemished Lamb already accepted for us (1 Pet 1:19).

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD... to be accepted you shall offer a male without blemish... Animals blind or disabled or mutilated or having a discharge or an itch or scabs you shall not offer to the LORD... You shall not profane my holy name, that I may be sanctified among the people of Israel. I am the LORD who sanctifies you.
verseByVerse.commentary: God turns from the priests to the offerings, and the rule is emphatic: they must be "without blemish." Nothing blind, injured, maimed, or diseased may be brought to the LORD; "it must be perfect to be accepted." Why does this matter so much? Because what we offer God reveals what we think of God. To bring the sickly animal you were going to lose anyway, the one you would never serve to an honored guest, is to say with your gift that God deserves your leftovers. Centuries later the prophet Malachi would blister Israel for exactly this sin: "When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not evil?... Present that to your governor; will he accept you?" (Mal 1:8). If you wouldn't insult a human official with such a gift, how dare you insult God? God is worthy of the first and the best, always. And there is a deeper reason the offering had to be flawless: every spotless lamb was a portrait of the one truly unblemished Sacrifice to come. Peter says we were ransomed "with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Pet 1:19). All these perfect animals were pointing to the one perfect Lamb, the only offering God ever fully accepted — and accepted in our place. Now, resting in him, we give God our best not to buy his favor, but because we already have it: "I am the LORD who sanctifies you."

23.title: The Feasts of the LORD: A Rehearsal of Redemption
23.text: <sup>2</sup>Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, These are the appointed feasts of the LORD that you shall proclaim as holy convocations; they are my appointed feasts... <sup>4</sup>These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them.
23.overview:
Chapter 23 lays out the sacred calendar of Israel — the appointed feasts of the LORD. These are not merely religious holidays; they are, as the Hebrew suggests, divine appointments, fixed meetings between God and his people. And taken together, the festal calendar is nothing less than a year-long rehearsal of redemption, a prophetic drama enacted annually, every feast a shadow whose substance is Christ (Col 2:16–17).

The cycle runs through the year: the weekly Sabbath; Passover and Unleavened Bread in the spring; Firstfruits; the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) fifty days later; then in the autumn, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles). Each marks a moment in Israel's life with God — and each, the New Testament reveals, finds its fulfillment in the gospel.

Watch the pattern emerge. Passover: "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7). Unleavened Bread: the sinless purity of the One offered and the new life we live in him. Firstfruits: "Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20) — and indeed Christ rose on the very day of Firstfruits. Weeks/Pentecost: fifty days after the resurrection, the Spirit was poured out (Acts 2), the harvest of the church begun. The spring feasts were fulfilled in Christ's first coming with stunning precision, often to the very day.

And the autumn feasts await: Trumpets, the gathering call; the Day of Atonement, the final reckoning; Booths, the ingathering and God dwelling with his people — pointing forward to Christ's return, the final judgment and atonement applied, and the eternal Feast of Tabernacles when "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Rev 21:3). The whole calendar is the gospel written in time. Carson notes that to read Leviticus 23 with New Testament eyes is to watch the shadows resolve into the face of Christ. The feasts were never about the rituals themselves; they were arrows pointing to him.

sections.title: The Sabbath and the Passover
sections.commentary:
The calendar begins with the weekly Sabbath (23:3) — the rhythm of rest that frames all the feasts — and then the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread (23:4–8), commemorating the night the destroyer passed over the blood-marked homes and Israel was delivered from Egypt. Paul makes the fulfillment explicit: "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Let us therefore celebrate the festival... with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 5:7–8).

The Passover lamb, its blood shielding from death, was always pointing to the Lamb of God. And remarkably, Christ was crucified at Passover — the shadow and the substance meeting on the same day. Sproul marveled that the timing was no accident but the precision of divine providence.

sections.title: Firstfruits and the Feast of Weeks
sections.commentary:
The Feast of Firstfruits (23:9–14) celebrated the first sheaf of the harvest, a pledge of the full harvest to come. Christ rose from the dead as "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor 15:20) — and rose on the very day of Firstfruits. His resurrection is the guarantee of ours; the first sheaf promises the whole harvest of the redeemed.

Fifty days later came the Feast of Weeks, or Pentecost (23:15–21), celebrating the wheat harvest. And on that day, fifty days after the resurrection, the Spirit was poured out upon the church (Acts 2), and three thousand souls were gathered in a single day — the firstfruits of the great harvest of the nations. The agricultural feast became the birthday of the church. Even the gleaning law reappears here (23:22), binding worship to mercy for the poor.

sections.title: The Autumn Feasts: Trumpets, Atonement, Booths
sections.commentary:
The autumn feasts gather the year toward its climax. The Feast of Trumpets (23:23–25) sounded the call to assembly. The Day of Atonement (23:26–32), the solemn day of affliction and cleansing, we have already seen fulfilled in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice (ch 16; Heb 9–10). The Feast of Booths (23:33–43), when Israel dwelt in tents to remember the wilderness and rejoice in the harvest, looks forward to the consummation.

Many see in the unfulfilled autumn feasts a foreshadowing of Christ's second coming: the trumpet that gathers his people (1 Thess 4:16), the final application of atonement, and the great ingathering when God will tabernacle with his people forever — "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them" (Rev 21:3). The whole calendar arcs from redemption accomplished to redemption consummated, and Christ is its beginning and its end.

23.theology:
The feasts as gospel shadows. Every feast is 'a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ' (Col 2:17) — the festal calendar is a rehearsal of redemption.

The spring feasts fulfilled. Passover (1 Cor 5:7), Firstfruits (1 Cor 15:20), and Pentecost (Acts 2) were fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit, often to the very day.

The autumn feasts awaited. Trumpets, Atonement, and Booths foreshadow Christ's return, final judgment, and the eternal dwelling of God with his people (Rev 21:3).
23.examples:
Then: Israel kept the rhythm of sacred feasts through the year, remembering deliverance, celebrating harvest, and being cleansed — unknowingly rehearsing the gospel in time.

Now: We see the feasts fulfilled in Christ our Passover, our Firstfruits, the giver of the Spirit at Pentecost — and we await the final ingathering when God will tabernacle with us forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares the appointed feasts (moadim): the weekly Sabbath; Passover and Unleavened Bread; Firstfruits; Weeks/Pentecost; Trumpets/Rosh Hashanah; the Day of Atonement; Booths/Tabernacles. Each feast is a holy convocation, a rehearsal of God's redemptive acts, and a prophetic anticipation of future fulfillment.
verseByVerse.theology: The appointed feasts are God's calendar — times when he meets with his people in covenant commemoration and anticipation. Every feast rehearses an act of redemption (Passover = the Exodus; Firstfruits = resurrection; Pentecost = the Spirit; Tabernacles = the wilderness and the coming kingdom) and anticipates a greater fulfillment. Paul's declaration in Colossians 2:17 — these are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ — applies to the entire feast calendar. Jesus is the Passover lamb (1 Cor. 5:7), the Firstfruits of resurrection (1 Cor. 15:20), the gift of Pentecost (Acts 2), and the Tabernacles coming king (Rev. 21:3).
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson writes that the feast calendar is the gospel in advance: each appointed season is God announcing, before the events, what the events will mean. The Israelite who kept the feasts was rehearsing the redemption that God would accomplish in Christ. The Christian who understands the feasts is reading the Old Testament gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at the time appointed for them. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at twilight, is the LORD's Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word moadim — appointed feasts, fixed times, set appointments — reveals the character of the feast calendar. These are not suggestions or commemorations that Israel may observe if convenient; they are appointments, times when God has committed to meet with his people. The entire year is structured around these meetings with God: Passover and Unleavened Bread in the spring (redemption commemorated), Firstfruits and Weeks at harvest (God's provision and the gift of the Spirit), Trumpets and Atonement and Tabernacles in the fall (judgment, cleansing, and dwelling). The year is a covenant narrative: redeemed, sustained, judged, cleansed, and finally dwelling with God. The church lives in the already of Christ's fulfillment and the not-yet of his return, celebrating the feasts' realities in baptism and the Lord's Supper until he comes.

24.title: The Lampstand, the Bread, and the Holiness of the Name
24.text: <sup>2</sup>Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly. <sup>5</sup>You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it... <sup>8</sup>Every Sabbath day Aaron shall arrange it before the LORD regularly...
24.overview:
Chapter 24 sets two beautiful images of continual ministry — the lampstand and the bread of the Presence — alongside a sobering account of judgment on blasphemy. At first the juxtaposition seems jarring, but together they teach that the God who provides continual light and bread for his people will not have his name dishonored.

The golden lampstand was to burn continually, tended with pure oil morning and evening (24:1–4), a light that never went out in the Holy Place. And on the table stood twelve loaves, the bread of the Presence, set out fresh every Sabbath, one for each tribe (24:5–9) — Israel continually represented before God, continually sustained. Light and bread, perpetually before the face of God: these are the great symbols of God's provision for his people's life and seeing.

And both find their fulfillment in Christ. "I am the light of the world," he declared; "whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life" (John 8:12). The lampstand that never went out points to the light that the darkness has not overcome (John 1:5). And "I am the bread of life," he said; "whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). The bread of the Presence, ever before God, points to the One who is our continual sustenance and who keeps us continually present before the Father. Begg loves to note that we live by light and bread — and Christ is both.

Then comes the account of the blasphemer who cursed the Name and was stoned (24:10–23). The contrast is deliberate: the God who gives light and bread is the God whose name is holy. To blaspheme the Name is to despise the very Giver of life. The chapter, and the famous "eye for eye" principle (24:20) — which was a limit on vengeance, not a license for it — drive home the seriousness of dishonoring God. And it points us to Christ, who, when he was reviled and falsely charged with blasphemy, did not revile in return (1 Pet 2:23), but bore the curse of the Name-breakers, so that we who have dishonored God's name might hallow it and be hallowed by it.

sections.title: The Continual Light
sections.commentary:
Pure oil from beaten olives keeps the lampstand burning "regularly" before the LORD (24:2–4). The light never goes out in the Holy Place. Ferguson notes the symbolism: God provides a light that does not fail, a constant illumination in his presence.

Christ is the fulfillment: "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). And he makes his people lights too — "You are the light of the world" (Matt 5:14) — burning with borrowed radiance, fueled by the oil of the Spirit, that the light may never go out in the dark world.

sections.title: The Bread of the Presence
sections.commentary:
Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out fresh every Sabbath before the LORD (24:5–8). Israel is continually represented before God, continually sustained. The bread is "a memorial portion... a food offering to the LORD" (24:7), a perpetual covenant.

Christ is the bread of life (John 6:35), the One who keeps his people ever before the Father and ever nourished. Calvin saw in the twelve loaves the whole people of God held continually in the presence of God — a picture fulfilled as Christ presents us, complete in him, before the Father's face. We are never out of God's sight, never beyond his sustaining grace.

sections.title: The Holiness of the Name
sections.commentary:
A man of mixed parentage blasphemes the Name in a quarrel and is put to death by stoning (24:10–16, 23). The severity is jarring, but the point is clear: the God who provides light and bread is holy, and his name is not to be cursed. The third commandment — "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain" (Exod 20:7) — is enforced.

The "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" principle (24:19–20) appears here as a principle of proportionate justice, limiting vengeance rather than licensing it. Jesus would later transcend it, calling his people not to retaliation but to mercy (Matt 5:38–39) — fulfilling, not abolishing, its true intent. And Christ himself, falsely accused of blasphemy and reviled, "when he was reviled... did not revile in return" (1 Pet 2:23). He bore the curse of those who curse the Name, that we might learn to hallow it: "Hallowed be your name" (Matt 6:9).

24.theology:
Christ the light. The continual lampstand points to Jesus, 'the light of the world' (John 8:12), and to his people who shine with borrowed light (Matt 5:14).

Christ the bread. The bread of the Presence points to Jesus, 'the bread of life' (John 6:35), who keeps us continually present and nourished before the Father.

The holiness of the Name. The judgment on the blasphemer enforces reverence for God's name; Christ, reviled, bore the curse of Name-breakers that we might hallow it (1 Pet 2:23; Matt 6:9).
24.examples:
Then: The priests tended a light that never went out and set fresh bread before God each Sabbath, while Israel learned that the name of the holy God must never be cursed.

Now: We live by Christ our light and bread, kept continually before the Father, and we hallow the Name we once dishonored — for Christ bore its curse and teaches us to pray, 'Hallowed be your name.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-23 - The Lamp, the Bread, and the Blasphemer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lamp in the tent of meeting must be tended continually. The twelve loaves of bread of the Presence are placed before the LORD every Sabbath. Then a narrative: a man of mixed Israelite-Egyptian heritage blasphemes the Name. God commands he be stoned. The lex talionis is re-stated: life for life, eye for eye.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy narrative in the middle of ritual regulations is jarring — but the juxtaposition is intentional. The lamp burns continually in God's presence; the Name is holy; and the man who blasphemes the Name meets the consequence. The Name of God is not casual religious vocabulary; it is the self-revelation of the Holy One. To blaspheme it is to assault God's own self-disclosure. The lex talionis that follows is not vindictiveness; it is the covenant principle that every offense carries a proportional consequence, and the greatest offense carries the greatest consequence.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur notes that the penalty for blasphemy required witnesses to lay their hands on the blasphemer's head before the stoning — mirroring the laying of hands on the sacrifice. The blasphemer who assaulted the holiness of God was himself the sacrifice, bearing his own guilt, covered by no atonement because he had rejected the Name that is the source of all atonement.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death. All the congregation shall stone him. The sojourner as well as the native, when he blasphemes the Name, shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary: The bread of the Presence — twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set before the LORD every Sabbath, eaten by the priests in the Holy Place — is the covenant meal maintained in God's presence all week, every week. It says: Israel is always before God; the twelve tribes are always in his sight. The blasphemer who interrupts this calm order of covenant worship is dealt with immediately and definitively. The law applies equally to sojourner and native — the stranger who lives among Israel is subject to the same covenant obligations. The Name — YHWH, the I AM — is not available for abuse by anyone, insider or outsider. The holiness of God's name is the covenant protection of God's self-revelation, and to assault it is to assault the covenant itself.

25.title: The Jubilee: The Year of the LORD's Favor
25.text: <sup>10</sup>And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 unveils one of the most radical and beautiful institutions in all of Scripture: the Sabbatical Year and, every fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Every seventh year the land rested and debts were eased; but every fiftieth year, the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement and liberty was proclaimed throughout the land — slaves set free, debts cancelled, ancestral lands restored to their original families. A whole society pressed the reset button. The poor were lifted, the enslaved were liberated, the dispossessed came home.

The theology beneath it is breathtaking: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (25:23). Israel did not ultimately own the land; God did. They were tenants of his grace. Therefore no debt could be permanent, no slavery perpetual, no family forever dispossessed — because everything belonged to God, and God is a Redeemer. The Jubilee was grace written into the economic order, a structural mercy, a society shaped by the character of a liberating God.

And then, in the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus stood up, opened the scroll of Isaiah, and read words steeped in the language of Jubilee: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to proclaim liberty to the captives... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:18–19). Then he rolled up the scroll and said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). Jesus declared himself the true Jubilee. He is the liberty for the captives, the release for the debtors, the homecoming for the dispossessed. Every slave he frees, every debt he cancels, every exile he brings home.

Keller loved to preach that the gospel is the ultimate Jubilee: our debt of sin — which we could never repay — is cancelled entirely; our slavery to sin is broken; our lost inheritance is restored; and we who were strangers are brought home to the family of God. And the Jubilee that Christ inaugurated will be consummated in the new creation, the everlasting year of the Lord's favor, when all things are restored and the whole earth rests in the freedom of the children of God. The trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — for it is by the blood of the cross that our true Jubilee is bought. Liberty, at last, throughout the land.

sections.title: The Sabbath of the Land
sections.commentary:
Every seventh year the land itself was to rest — no sowing, no reaping, a Sabbath for the soil (25:1–7). The people had to trust God to provide. This taught radical dependence: the same lesson as the manna, that man does not live by his own labor alone but by the provision of God.

Calvin notes that the Sabbath year trained Israel to trust the LORD's provision over their own striving. It is a rebuke to the anxious, grasping, never-resting spirit of fallen humanity, and a call to the rest of faith that finds its fullness in Christ, who says, "Come to me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

sections.title: The Year of Jubilee: Liberty Proclaimed
sections.commentary:
Every fiftieth year, on the Day of Atonement, the trumpet sounded and Jubilee was proclaimed: "proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants" (25:10). Slaves freed, debts released, ancestral lands returned. It is no accident that the Jubilee trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — liberty flows from atonement; freedom is bought by blood.

This is the very text echoed in Isaiah 61 and read by Jesus at Nazareth (Luke 4:18–21). Keller called the gospel the ultimate Jubilee: the unpayable debt of sin cancelled, the chains of bondage struck off, the lost inheritance restored, the exile brought home. "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" — Jesus is the Jubilee in person.

sections.title: The Land Is Mine: A Theology of Redemption
sections.commentary:
The foundation is laid bare: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (25:23). Because everything belongs to God, no loss is permanent, and the figure of the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) emerges — the near relative who buys back lost land or frees an enslaved kinsman (25:25, 47–49). This is the role Boaz plays for Ruth, and the role, supremely, that Christ plays for us.

Carson observes that the kinsman-redeemer points unmistakably to Jesus, who took on our flesh to become our near kinsman (Heb 2:11–17) and redeemed us — bought us back — not with silver but with his own blood (1 Pet 1:18–19). The Jubilee theology of redemption finds its center in the Redeemer who restores our lost inheritance and brings us home. The whole chapter is a meditation on the God who will not let his people stay enslaved, indebted, or dispossessed forever.

25.theology:
The gospel as Jubilee. Liberty for captives, cancelled debts, restored inheritance — fulfilled in Christ who proclaimed 'the year of the Lord's favor' (Luke 4:18-21) as accomplished in himself.

'The land is mine.' All belongs to God (25:23); we are sojourners of his grace, which is why no debt or bondage is permanent under his rule.

The kinsman-redeemer. The go'el who buys back lost land and frees the enslaved points to Christ, our near kinsman who redeemed us with his blood (Heb 2:14-17; 1 Pet 1:18-19).
25.examples:
Then: Every fiftieth year the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, and across Israel slaves went free, debts were cancelled, and families returned to their lost lands — grace built into the social order.

Now: Jesus is our Jubilee. He cancels the unpayable debt of sin, breaks our slavery, restores our inheritance, and brings us home — and will consummate the everlasting year of the Lord's favor in the new creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-55 - The Sabbath Year and the Year of Jubilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every seventh year the land rests — no plowing, no harvesting, only what grows of itself. After seven sevens of years (forty-nine years), the fiftieth year is the Year of Jubilee: the trumpet sounds, all debts are cancelled, all enslaved Hebrews go free, all land returns to its original family. No permanent poverty is possible in Israel's covenant economy.
verseByVerse.theology: The Year of Jubilee is one of the most radical economic commands in human history. Every fifty years, all economic inequality is reset: the land cannot be permanently alienated from its family, the impoverished person cannot be permanently enslaved. The theology is explicit: the land is mine; you are sojourners and tenants with me (v.23). God is the ultimate landowner; all human property is stewardship under his ownership. Economic inequality is real and permitted — but it is never permanent. The covenant economy has a built-in correction. Jesus inaugurates his ministry by reading from Isaiah 61 — the Jubilee text — and declaring: Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. He is the ultimate Jubilee.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller calls the Year of Jubilee the most visionary social legislation in the ancient world. No other ancient legal code had a mechanism for systematic debt cancellation and land redistribution. The theology behind it — God owns everything, human ownership is stewardship, the poor are not permanently excluded from their inheritance — is the foundation of a just society.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.
verseByVerse.commentary: Liberty throughout the land — these words, inscribed on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, come from this verse. The Year of Jubilee begins with the sounding of the trumpet on the Day of Atonement: first the slate is wiped clean with God (Yom Kippur), then the slate is wiped clean with each other (Jubilee). The sequence is theologically necessary: you cannot restructure human relationships rightly without first being rightly related to God. The cancelled debts, the freed slaves, the returned land — these are not charity but justice, the covenant ordering of a community under God. No one permanently loses their inheritance; no one is permanently enslaved by misfortune. The Jubilee is the economic expression of resurrection: what was lost is restored; what was dead is made alive again.

26.title: Blessings and Curses: The Covenant's Heart
26.text: <sup>3</sup>If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them... <sup>12</sup>And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people... <sup>44</sup>Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them... <sup>45</sup>But I will for their sake remember the covenant with their forefathers.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 brings the covenant to its solemn climax with the great recital of blessings and curses — the two roads that lie before the covenant people. Covenant faithfulness brings blessing: rain in season, fruitful harvests, peace in the land, victory over enemies, and above all the crowning promise: "I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people" (26:12). Covenant unfaithfulness brings curse: in escalating waves, disease, drought, defeat, famine, and finally exile from the land. The structure mirrors the covenant treaties of the ancient world, but the heart of it is the presence or absence of God himself.

The escalating judgments are sobering — "sevenfold" again and again (26:18, 21, 24, 28), as God patiently, repeatedly disciplines a stubborn people. Yet even the curses are not vindictive; they are the disciplines of a covenant Father designed to bring his people to repentance. And here lies the chapter's astonishing grace: even when Israel is exiled in the land of their enemies, broken and scattered, God says, "if they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant" (26:40–42). "Yet for all that... I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44).

This is the heart of the matter: God's covenant faithfulness outlasts his people's faithlessness. Even in the deepest judgment, mercy has the last word, because the covenant rests finally not on Israel's obedience but on God's character. "I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:45). The God who threatens curse is the God who will not let his people go.

And the cross is where the curses and the blessings meet. For the dreadful truth is that Israel — and we — chose the road of unfaithfulness and earned every curse. But "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'" (Gal 3:13). On the cross, Jesus drank the full cup of covenant curse, every sevenfold judgment, the ultimate exile of God-forsakenness — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — so that the covenant blessing might come to us: "so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles" (Gal 3:14). He bore the curse; we receive the blessing. And the crowning promise of verse 12 finds its everlasting fulfillment: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Rev 21:3).

sections.title: The Blessings of Obedience
sections.commentary:
God promises rich blessing for covenant faithfulness — rain, harvest, peace, security, fruitfulness (26:3–10). But the summit of all blessing is relational: "I will make my dwelling among you... And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people" (26:11–12). The greatest blessing is not the gifts but the Giver, not the land but the LORD walking in their midst.

Ferguson notes that this is the refrain of the whole covenant — "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" — the heartbeat of redemption from Eden to the New Jerusalem. God's deepest desire is to dwell with his people, and our deepest blessing is to have him.

sections.title: The Curses of Disobedience
sections.commentary:
The curses unfold in escalating waves, each introduced by God's patient warning to discipline "sevenfold" if they will not turn (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Disease, drought, wild beasts, the sword, famine so severe it leads to horror, and finally exile and scattering among the nations (26:33). The land itself will keep its Sabbaths while the people are away (26:34–35).

Sproul observed that these curses are not the rage of a capricious deity but the covenant discipline of a holy God, designed to break a hardened people and drive them to repentance. The escalation reveals divine patience as much as divine justice — God warns and warns again before the final judgment of exile. Yet the curses are real, and they fell: the exile to Babylon was Leviticus 26 coming to pass.

sections.title: Mercy Has the Last Word
sections.commentary:
And then, astonishingly, grace breaks through the curses. "If they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant with Jacob" (26:40–42). Even in exile, the door of repentance stands open. And the ground of hope is not Israel's worthiness but God's faithfulness: "Yet for all that... I will not spurn them... I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:44–45).

This is the gospel's foundation: the covenant rests on God's character, not ours. Keller pressed that God's faithfulness outlasts our faithlessness, that mercy triumphs over judgment for all who confess. And the cross is where it all converges: Christ bore the full covenant curse (Gal 3:13) — the disease, the sword, the famine, the exile of God-forsakenness — so that we might inherit the covenant blessing and that God might dwell with us forever (Rev 21:3). The chapter that ends in mercy points to the cross where mercy was bought with blood.

26.theology:
The covenant's two roads. Blessing for faithfulness, curse for unfaithfulness — with the crowning blessing being God's own presence: 'I will walk among you... you shall be my people' (26:12).

Mercy outlasts judgment. Even in exile, confession reopens the door, for the covenant rests on God's faithfulness, not ours: 'I will for their sake remember the covenant' (26:45).

Christ bore the curse. Jesus 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us' (Gal 3:13), drinking the full covenant judgment so the blessing might come to us (Gal 3:14).
26.examples:
Then: Israel stood before two roads — blessing or curse — and was warned that unfaithfulness would bring escalating discipline and finally exile, yet promised that confession would meet a faithful, remembering God.

Now: We who earned every curse find that Christ drank it all on the cross, bearing even the exile of God-forsakenness, so that the covenant blessing is ours and God dwells with us forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 - Blessings for Obedience and Curses for Disobedience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant sanctions: abundant harvests, peace, victory, God's presence for obedience. Escalating judgments — disease, drought, defeat, terror, famine, exile, desolation — for disobedience. But if in exile they confess their sins, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus 26 is the covenant-sanction chapter — the blessings and curses that seal the covenant of Sinai. The pattern of escalating judgment (five rounds, each more severe) and the promised restoration upon repentance is the structure of Israel's entire subsequent history. The prophets will preach against the violations; the exile will come; and the covenant will survive because God cannot forget it. The final word of the chapter is not judgment but covenant-memory: I will remember my covenant with Jacob... I will not spurn them or abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them, for I am the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul notes that the blessings of Leviticus 26 are not wages but gifts: God is not obligated to bless obedience; he chooses to. The curses are also gifts in a different register: they are the loving discipline of a God who will not let his people comfortably settle for covenant-breaking. The entire history of Israel's discipline is the working out of this chapter — severe, sustained, and ultimately redemptive.

verseByVerse.quote: But if they confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers in their treachery that they committed against me, and also in walking contrary to me, so that I walked contrary to them and brought them into the land of their enemies — if then their uncircumcised heart is humbled and they make amends for their iniquity, then I will remember my covenant with Jacob, and I will remember my covenant with Isaac and my covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant-keeping faithfulness of God shines most brightly in this verse. Israel will break the covenant — repeatedly, catastrophically. But God's memory is longer than Israel's faithlessness. He will remember: the word zakhar occurs three times in this verse. He will remember Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, and the land. The covenant does not depend on Israel's faithfulness for its ultimate survival; it depends on God's faithfulness. This is why the entire Old Testament history is not a tragedy: the people fail, the judgments fall, but God remembers. And in the fullness of time, the Son of God comes — the faithful covenant partner that Israel never was — and in him the covenant is finally and fully fulfilled. The memory of God becomes the mercy of God becomes the mission of God in Christ.

27.title: Vows and Dedications: All Things Are His
27.text: <sup>28</sup>...every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD. <sup>30</sup>Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD. <sup>34</sup>These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
27.overview:
Leviticus closes not with the thunder of Sinai but with the quiet, voluntary devotion of the heart — laws about vows and dedications, the freewill consecration of persons, animals, houses, and land to the LORD. After all the commanded offerings, the book ends with the offerings that no one commands: the spontaneous overflow of a grateful heart that says, "All I have is yours, and I give it gladly."

The chapter provides a careful valuation system for redeeming what has been vowed (27:1–25), and reaffirms that the firstborn, the devoted thing, and the tithe already belong to the LORD (27:26–33). "Every tithe of the land... is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD" (27:30). The principle beneath it all is the great truth that crowns the whole book: everything belongs to God. "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof" (Ps 24:1). What we vow to him, we give back from what was already his.

Some have wondered why Leviticus, having reached its glorious heights in the Day of Atonement and the Jubilee, should end on such an administrative note. But there is a deep fittingness. The book that began with God calling sinners to draw near through sacrifice ends with redeemed sinners drawing near with their whole lives, voluntarily, joyfully consecrated. The proper response to all the grace of Leviticus — the offerings, the priesthood, the atonement, the holiness, the Jubilee — is the glad surrender of everything to God. Worship that begins with God's gift to us ends with our gift to God.

And it all points to Christ, who is both the One devoted wholly to God and the price of our redemption. He is the true tithe, the firstborn given to the Father, the One who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7), holding nothing back. And he is the ransom by which we, who could never pay our own valuation, are redeemed — "you were bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20). The book that opened with the burnt offering — total consecration — closes with the same call, now turned toward us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (Rom 12:1). Holy, holy, holy is the LORD — and all that we are and have is his.

sections.title: The Valuation of Persons
sections.commentary:
When someone vows a person to the LORD, a monetary valuation is set for redeeming the vow (27:1–8). Strikingly, provision is made for the poor: "if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him" (27:8). No one is shut out of devotion by poverty; the priest adjusts the price to what the person can afford.

Calvin notes the dignity this confers: every person has worth before God, and even the poorest may consecrate themselves. And the deeper truth presses in — we could never pay our own true valuation before God. The price of our redemption was beyond all silver and gold; it was "the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:19). We are valued not by what we can pay but by what Christ paid for us.

sections.title: Devoting Animals, Houses, and Land
sections.commentary:
Detailed regulations govern the dedication and redemption of animals, houses, and fields (27:9–25), with the recurring option to redeem a vowed thing by adding a fifth (27:13, 15, 19) — the same generous overpayment we saw in the guilt offering. The system protects against rash vows while honoring genuine devotion.

Begg notes the seriousness with which God treats our promises to him: a vow is not to be made lightly, for "it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay" (Eccl 5:5). Yet the heart of the chapter is the gladness of giving back to God what is his, the joyful consecration of the things of ordinary life — our property, our possessions, our place — to the Lord who gave them all.

sections.title: The Tithe Belongs to the LORD
sections.commentary:
The chapter, and the book, close by reaffirming what already belongs to God: the firstborn (27:26), the devoted thing which is "most holy to the LORD" (27:28), and the tithe — "every tithe of the land... is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD" (27:30). We do not give God a tithe as if the other ninety percent were ours; the tithe simply confesses that all of it is his.

So Leviticus ends where true worship always lands: "All things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (1 Chr 29:14). The book that began with sinners drawing near through blood ends with redeemed sinners consecrating their whole lives in glad surrender. And it all points to Christ, the firstborn devoted wholly to the Father (Heb 10:7), the ransom that redeemed us when we could not redeem ourselves (1 Cor 6:20). The final word of Leviticus calls us to present ourselves, body and soul, a living sacrifice to the holy God who has made us his own.

27.theology:
All things belong to God. The tithe and the devoted thing confess that everything is the LORD's (27:30; Ps 24:1); what we give, we give back from what was already his.

Voluntary consecration. The book ends with freewill devotion — the glad surrender of a redeemed heart, the fitting response to all the grace of Leviticus (Rom 12:1).

Christ our ransom. We could never pay our own valuation; we were redeemed by 'the precious blood of Christ' (1 Pet 1:19), the firstborn devoted wholly to the Father (Heb 10:7).
27.examples:
Then: An Israelite, moved by gratitude, might vow himself, his animals, his house, or his field to the LORD, and bring his tithe — confessing that all he had belonged to God.

Now: Having received all the grace of Leviticus, we present our whole selves to God as a living sacrifice. We give gladly because all is his, and because Christ first gave himself wholly for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Regulations for vows made to the LORD: the monetary equivalent for persons dedicated, animals, houses, and fields. The tithe of the land is holy to the LORD; the tithe of the herd and flock belongs to God — every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's staff.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus ends with the regulations for vows and tithes — the voluntary and the required giving back to God. The vow system provides a way for an Israelite to dedicate himself, his family, his property to the LORD; the redemption price provides a way to fulfill the spirit of the vow while remaining in the community. The tithe — ten percent of everything — is not the ceiling of generosity but the floor: the minimum acknowledgment that God owns everything and we return to him what is already his.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin observes that the tithe system teaches the fundamental covenant economics: all we have is God's; we return a portion as an acknowledgment of that ownership; we live on what remains as stewards of what God entrusts to us. The New Testament does not abolish this principle; it radicalizes it: each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). The minimum of the tithe is superseded by the maximum of cheerful grace-giving.

verseByVerse.quote: Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD... Every tithe of herds and flocks, every tenth animal of all that pass under the herdsman's staff, shall be holy to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tithe — every tenth — belongs to the LORD. Every tenth animal that passes under the shepherd's staff, regardless of quality, is counted off and set apart as holy. It is not the best tenth; it is the random tenth — the tenth animal in the sequence, whether good or bad, goes to God. The randomness is theologically significant: the tithe is not about giving God our surplus or our inferior animals; it is about giving God the first claim on our goods, without calculation of what is best to keep. Leviticus closes with this principle of holy ownership: the land is the LORD's, the animals are the LORD's, the firstborn are the LORD's, the tenth is the LORD's. The whole book has been teaching one thing, many ways: you belong to God. Everything you have is his. Live as those who know it.
